subtopic: MR. BALDWIN    STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE
MR. BALDWIN    STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE
speechtext:
At the opening of yesterday's sitting the hon. member for Peace River raised a question of privilege based upon the report of Wednesday's proceedings recorded at page 73 of Votes and Proceedings with regard to the motion for the production of papers in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Hon. members will recall that I reserved my decision at that time.
As was suggested by the Minister of Labour and by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre during the discussion which followed, it would seem there are two points involved in the question raised by the hon. member for Peace River. In the first instance there is a point of order in regard to the regularity of the proceedings on Wednesday last, and in the second place an alleged question of privilege.
Allow me to deal first with the reference made to the purported irregularity in procedure in the case under review. Paragraph 1, citation 70 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, reads in part as follows:
Points of order are questions raised with the view of calling attention to any departure from the standing orders or the customary modes of proceeding in debate or in the conduct of legislative business, . . .
Paragraph 4 of the same citation reads as follows:
A point of order against procedure must be raised promptly and before the question has passed to a stage at which the objection would be out of place.
It is my view that it would be inappropriate for me to discuss at this time the regularity or otherwise of the procedure followed in this case last Wednesday since, as was stated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, "What happened yesterday, happened; we cannot turn the clock back.".
Perhaps I might make a further comment with regard to this point before leaving it. Standing order 35 reads in part as follows:
No member may reflect upon any vote of the house, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.	[DOT]
28902-5-49i
Now, a vote was taken and duly recorded in Votes and Proceedings of Wednesday last on this question. It seems to me that the last part of the discussion which took place yesterday was in contravention of the provisions of this standing order 35.
We come now to the second point which the hon. member for Peace River designated as a question of privilege based upon the report of Wednesday's proceedings as recorded at page 73 of Votes and Proceedings for Wednesday last. The hon. gentleman referred to a ruling or a statement by one of my very worthy predecessors in 1961 concerning the practice of this house in regard to the acceptance of motions for papers under certain reservations. The hon. member referred also to a motion which had been proposed on Wednesday last by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and which was accepted by the Minister without Portfolio subject to certain reservations, but which was recorded in Votes and Proceedings as adopted by the house without conditions or reservations attached thereto.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre also drew attention to three other motions which also were adopted on Wednesday last under certain reservations, but which also were not so recorded in Votes and Proceedings for that day. There is, I suggest, a notable distinction to be made between the question under review and the other precedents referred to.
1.	In the four cases referred to the member proposing the motion accepted the reservation expressed in each case by a minister.
2.	I think this is the significant point, that the house concurred in the arrangement or agreement without dissenting voice.
3.	In effect one must presume that arrangements were made, by unanimous consent, in all four cases.
4.	In these procedures there was no division of opinion in the house and, consequently, no division of opinion should or could have been recorded in Votes and Proceedings.
Let us now return to the proceedings under review, and I must say at this stage that so far as I have been able to determine in the time at my disposal, we had a unprecedented procedure on Wednesday. In this case we had a division of opinion. The

Question of Privilege
procedure was challenged and put to a vote. May I briefly review the procedure followed on that occasion.
1.	When the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was called, the Secretary of State for External Affairs intervened and expressed the government's reservations with regard to the production of certain papers.
2.	After a number of interventions by several hon. members the proposer of the motion, the hon. gentleman from Winnipeg North Centre, concluded as reported at page 689 of Hansard by saying:
I understood that the minister was prepared to let the motion pass subject to his reservation. Those are the words the minister used, and I am prepared to accept the reservations he has now made. Obviously if the return that is brought down is not satisfactory I can ask further questions, but it seems to me that as the mover of the motion I have the right to suggest that I am prepared to accept the passing of it subject to the reservations the minister has now made.
3.	Thereupon the Chair put the motion in the following words:
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the said motion subject to the reservations or remarks of the minister?
Hansard reports what immediately followed, as follows:

4.	After hon. members were called in, Hansard records the procedure as follows:

subtopic: MR. BALDWIN    STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Order. The question is as follows. Mr. Knowles, seconded by Mr. Douglas, moves:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this house a copy of any documents, communications, correspondence or other papers, dated since June 10, 1957, containing any commitments by the Government of Canada to accept or acquire nuclear weapons for Canadian forces, -subject to the reservations of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Those in favour of the motion, please rise.

subtopic: MR. BALDWIN    STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I might rise, I suggest that the reservations be included in the motion. It is very important those reservations be there because we are asking for the complete record not the expurgated record.

subtopic: MR. BALDWIN    STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE
speechtext:
The suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition is interesting, but I do think the record speaks for itself and I think the minister should take his own responsibilities and not the Speaker.

Therefore unless there is serious objection I propose to put the motion as I have read it. Those in favour of the motion will please rise.
To decide whether there is before the house a bona fide point of privilege, and this is the only question which is before me at this time, we must ask ourselves if the entry in Votes and Proceedings reflects the proceeding which took place in the house at that time. The entry at page 73 of Votes and Proceedings for Wednesday, June 5, 1963 reads in part as follows:
And the question being put, the said motion, subject to the reservations expressed by the honourable the Secretary of State for External Affairs, was agreed to on the following division:
I submit after a careful scrutiny of the record, as reported in Hansard, it is my humble opinion that the entry in Votes and Proceedings accurately reflects the procedure on the motion proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. That being so, I am regretfully unable to accept the submission of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) as a bona fide question of privilege.
In terminating my remarks may I offer a suggestion to hon. members of this house. As several hon. members pointed out during yesterday's discussion, it has been a practice for some years past not to record in Votes and Proceedings any reservations expressed by ministers in regard to such motions. However, in the light of the altered circumstances that developed on Wednesday and again yesterday, the house may now be of the opinion that reservations by ministers should be recorded in Votes and Proceedings in every case. It may be that the proposed committee on procedure would like to review the question and recommend a course of procedure for the consideration of the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, on Tuesday of this week the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) asked this question of the Minister of Fisheries as reported at page 625 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, would the minister be kind enough to complete the record by giving us the names of the members of the advisory commission?
This referred to the advisory commission to the Canadian fisheries delegation going to Washington. On Wednesday last, as reported at page 693 of Hansard, I reminded the minister that he had said he would give the names and asked if he was ready to do so. The minister replied:

Mr. Speaker, I do not have with me the information concerning the six members of the advisory committee, but I will have it on Friday when I get back from Washington.
Apparently a member of the press gallery, Mr. Murphy of radio station CKNW, New Westminster, obtained this information from the minister's office yesterday and broadcast it in the lower mainland of British Columbia. I should like to know the explanation for this, since this information has not yet been given to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minister of Fisheries):
maintopic: MR. PRITTIE-INFORMATION GIVEN TO PRESS BEFORE BEING GIVEN TO MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is certainly no question of privilege in the matter that has been raised by the hon. member. I stated on Wednesday, when I was asked to supply the names of the members of the advisory committee to the north Pacific fisheries commission, that I did not at the time have the information with me in the house and that if the hon. member was interested I would give him the names on Friday.
There is no breach of privilege. The names were available. They had been made public in Vancouver, when the meeting was held last week, by representatives of the department with members of the north Pacific fisheries commission.

subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING WITH U.S. SECRETARY OF DEFENCE

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Defence Production):
subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING WITH U.S. SECRETARY OF DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, realizing the interest of hon. members of the house in the

Inquiries of the Ministry continuation Of our satisfactory relationship with the United States in matters of industrial production for defence purposes and co-operation therein, I should like to make a brief report on a meeting I had yesterday in Washington with the secretary of defence of the United States. Our meeting was held in a spirit of great cordiality and reaffirmed positively the intention of both our countries to continue to support a defence production sharing program. Assurances were given that the difficulties experienced by both countries in respect of balance of payments problems should not be allowed to interfere with the continuation and enlargement of this program.
It was recognized that both countries have balance of payments problems. However, it was agreed that such problems must not interfere with our joint production sharing objectives. The maintenance of a general balance in our reciprocal cross-border procurement of equipment seems the best answer to concern at the drain on foreign exchange reserves through such procurement. To this end it was agreed that production sharing will not be limited by the so-called balance of payments directives issued by the secretary of defence of the United States, and that full consideration will be given to all qualified Canadian sources.
The house will appreciate that the trend of increasing costs and complexity for military equipment emphasizes the necessity for joint research, development and production In line with the agreed NATO concept of interdependence for our common defence.
For the future, as in the past, Canada expects to procure from United States defence industry those items which it does not make economic sense to try to produce in Canada. In return we look to continuing opportunities for Canadian industry to supply United States defence requirements where Canadian companies can compete on the basis of price, quality and delivery.

subtopic: FIVE YEAR MORATORIUM ON APPLICATIONS FOR ABANDONMENT

speakeroldname: Mr. R. R. Southam (Moose Mountain) moved
subtopic: FIVE YEAR MORATORIUM ON APPLICATIONS FOR ABANDONMENT
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-70, to amend the Railway Act (abandonment moratorium).

subtopic: FIVE YEAR MORATORIUM ON APPLICATIONS FOR ABANDONMENT
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: FIVE YEAR MORATORIUM ON APPLICATIONS FOR ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the magnitude of the problem of railway abandonment is becoming apparent from the large mass of applications being directed to the board of transport commissioners based on recommendations of the McPherson royal commission on transportation. These abandonments are estimated to affect between 4,300 and 8,600 miles of branch lines. About 4,000 to 5,000 miles of this total is in the three prairie provinces, and 2,000 miles is in Saskatchewan.
The purpose of this bill is to declare a moratorium of five years on all applications respecting rail abandonment accepted and granted by the board of transport commissioners so that private persons, rural and urban municipalities, primary producers, industries, businesses, elevator companies, wheat pools, labour organizations, the motor transport and pipe line industries and all others which may be adversely affected may plan well in advance before the abandonment actually takes place, in this way alleviating as far as possible the social and economic upheaval that may occur in many communities, especially those in rural areas. I hope this bill will receive widespread support from all parties in the house.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Inquiries of the Ministry Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. It is an urgent one regarding the government resolution on the order paper to divide the Northwest Territories into two separate territories.

The house resumed from Thursday, June 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That a special committee be appointed to consider matters relating to defence and to report from time to time its observations and opinions thereon; that the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses; that it be empowered to adjourn from place to place; that standing order 67 be suspended in relation to the committee; and that the committee consist of 24 members to be designated by the house at a later date.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating a simple resolution to set up a defence committee. We are not, within the terms of that resolution, debating defence or foreign policy. I recall, Mr. Speaker as no doubt you and other members of the house recall, that in the past, when the previous government was in office, whenever resolutions to set up committees were before the house, every time we on the opposition side attempted to discuss anything which could have been considered as of substance, the hon. member who represented Eglinton in those days was on his feet in an instant to insist that the debate should be restricted to the exact terms of the resoluion to set up the committee. On this occasion very wide latitude has been allowed, and I am not complaining about that at all. The whole subject of defence has come under review by members of the opposition together with various aspects of foreign policy which have nothing whatever to do with the subject matter of this resolution.

It has been suggested by speakers opposite, including the Leader of the Opposition that somehow or other this government has been limiting or preventing the discussion in this house not only of decisions before they have been made by the government-which would not be the normal constitutional practice, anyway

but has been limiting and even preventing the discussion of defence policy generally. In this connection it is interesting to note that we are now on the seventh day of defence discussions in this session of parliament which has not yet lasted one month; that there has been a subamendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne which dealt directly with this matter and on which a decision was reached with regard to one aspect of defence, namely the acceptance of nuclear arms, and that since then, during the discussion of this resolution, there has been ample opportunity for members to express their views on any aspect of defence.
This is the seventh day of the discussion of defence matters in this short session. It is also interesting to recall that in the previous years 1960-61, 1961-62 and 1962-63, there were only in the aggregate eight days in the House of Commons devoted to defence. Eight days in three years. We have had seven days in less than one month. I say deliberately that any charge-and such a charge has been made-* that we are trying to limit discussion and push these matters under the rug cannot be sustained.
During these last three days, which are quite a contrast to the situation in the previous parliament, we have discussed various aspects of the defence policy of this country. In respect of the suggestion made that this government has somehow or other been limiting the right of members of the House of Commons to discuss such matters and the charge that we have been making decisions- and I will deal with this later-without parliament knowing about them, I would recall, Mr. Speaker, that some very important decisions were made by the previous government in this field of defence, not only without this parliament having a chance at the time to discuss them before the decisions were made, but in some cases parliament only learned of them months or even years after they were made.
In 1957 a decision was taken at the NATO council, participated in and supported by the Canadian delegation of that day, for NATO to take on a nuclear role in collective defence. That decision was made in December, 1957 by the NATO council, and it was referred to only many months later. I am thinking now of the hearings before the defence committee on June 17, 1960, when the minister of defence of that day said that the use of

Appointment of Defence Committee atomic weapons in the event of attack has been recognized by the NATO council. Parliament was not consulted about that. Parliament was not even informed of that before the decision was taken, or indeed immediately afterwards. He-that is, Mr. Pearkes-also said at the same hearing on July 7 that the possibility of having to use nuclear weapons has been part of accepted NATO policy, and Canada participated in that decision at that time.
Then in 1959 a decision was made, and it was a decision, from which this whole much debated question of commitments arises, taken by the government of the day, in consultation with its NATO allies in Paris, and before this parliament was informed, to convert the Royal Canadian Air Force interceptor air division into an air division which would be given the role of strike reconnaissance. That is when it all began, in 1959.
Later, when on the estimates of the department of defence there was an opportunity to discuss this question, this party, in opposition at the time, made its position perfectly clear in regard to that role. It will be recalled by any hon. member who was in the house at the time, or if he does not recall it he can read Hansard, that one of the criticisms of that role by us at that time was that it would impose on our air division a role which could only be discharged by the use of nuclear weapons, including-and this was the expression we used-"baby bombs". There was no denial at that time from the government of that day that this was indeed the new role to be undertaken by the Royal Canadian Air Force abroad with NATO.
Then at the end of 1962 there was a NATO council meeting in Athens, I think it was, when there was laid down what we later learned from the press-again there was no discussion of it in parliament at that time

what has been called since that time the "guide lines" for the use and control of nuclear weapons inside NATO. Those were important decisions, decisions which bear on what we now call the commitments undertaken by the previous government. Those decisions were made and were not discussed in this House of Commons either before or immediately after they were made. So, Mr. Speaker, that surely disposes of the argument, if you can call it an argument, that we are not permitting sufficient discussion of these matters in the House of Commons and that we have made decisions before we have referred them to the House of Commons.
So far as the attitude of the parties in the house is concerned toward the setting up of this defence committee, it is quite clear from the debate which is now being wound up that

Appointment of Defence Committee the Social Credit and New Democratic parties approve of the establishment of a defence committee of this kind. The Conservative party, as far as one can gather, do not approve of it. Indeed, some members have definitely opposed it.
Mr. Speaker, I stated yesterday that we were supporting the setting up of this committee.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Read Hansard.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to learn that the Leader of the Opposition now supports the setting up of a defence policy committee, something which, when he had the responsibility of government, he rejected as invalid, unconstitutional, improper, and quite contrary to all our parliamentary practices.
That is what the Prime Minister always said.
I am delighted that the right hon. gentleman has now seen the light of opposition-
And the Prime Minister has seen the light of government.

-and I am sure that he and his party will make a useful contribution to the committee which in turn I hope will make a useful contribution toward clarifying policies and questions of defence. I hope that for the membership of this committee there will be an opportunity, as I know there will be, to get the kind of information that is available in regard to defence matters. There will be a disposition, I am sure, on the part of the committee, as there will be on the part of the government, not to sweep anything under the rug. If this committee is to be effective it must have all the information which can be given to it.
The only reservation, a reservation we must make, though some hon. gentlemen opposite have quarrelled with it, particularly the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) last evening, is that of national security and classified information which bears upon national security. I am quite sure that any hon. member of this house who has the interests of his country at heart would accept that kind of reservation, which is accepted in consideration given to defence matters by any free parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I hope it will be possible to put on this committee those members of the house who have had experience of, and shown interest in, defence matters. Certainly the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) will be able to make a most
[Mr. Pearson.)
useful contribution, and I have no doubt that he will be nominated by his party.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What type of experience in defence matters?

Some worry was expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) that perhaps we would not allow this committee to deal with policy; that we were somehow concealing the possibility of the committee dealing with policy matters. When I asked him, in order to clear this matter up, if he would move an amendment so as to make it clear beyond any possible shadow of doubt and include the words "including defence policy", he said that he would take that suggestion under advisement. No such amendment has been moved, and indeed no such amendment, Mr. Speaker, is necessary.
Then why move it?

"Why move it" is a good question. It would never have occurred to anybody to move it if doubts had not been raised by the hon. member to whom I referred, who alleged that we said we would not permit the committee to deal with defence policy. Then when I challenged him to make that amendment if he had any doubts, he abdicated that position.
You made the commitment.

The leader of the Social Credit party made some interesting suggestions as to matters that could be submitted and I hope will be submitted to and discussed by the committee. He made the point, as have other members opposite, which is certainly valid, that if the discussion in this committee is going to be effective it must go beyond the limit of defence in the narrow military sense. That point was also made last night by one or two speakers on the other side and, of course, it is quite impossible to understand all the implications of defence policy and have a committee of this kind do the job we hope it will do unless the relationship is recognized between defence policy and foreign policy.
At times it is impossible to disentangle the two aspects of defence. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) said that a committee of this kind should discuss the nature and magnitude of the threat to peace and security. That is an aspect of foreign policy as it is an aspect of defence policy, and I have no doubt the committee may wish to go into that. He suggested also, as have other members, that questions of specialization and standardization of. defence equipment and defence matters within the alliance should be
7S3

considered. He also said, and this was reiterated last night by the hon. member for Oxford, that we should examine how foreign policy and trade policy, economic policy, economic relationships, bear on defence policy. This is a matter of very great importance, of course, and NATO itself recognizes that interrelationship.
The leader of the New Democratic party made the point that in a committee of this kind the consideration of defence must be broad in that defence is, to quote his words, "much broader than nuclear arms". This is something we are apt to forget in the immediate controversies over nuclear arms. After all, nuclear weapons and nuclear defence are only one aspect of military defence.
It is hoped, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the suspicions and doubts that have been thrown on this, that this committee will be able to operate on as non-partisan a basis as is possible in dealing with a matter which does arouse controversy, which does arouse differences and tends to arouse passion.
The Leader of the Opposition raised a good many points in his statement yesterday. Some of these points were raised by other members, and I propose to try to deal with them during the remainder of my remarks. Perhaps before I do that I should mention specifically one subject which has been referred to by more than one speaker and notably by the leader of the New Democratic party, when he talked about the danger of our Atlantic coalition relying too much on the strategic nuclear deterrent as the protection of the peace, because that is all it can be expected to do. If the strategic nuclear force is ever called into action it will have failed in its purpose, and nothing then will be able to save us from the devastation, tragedy and catastrophe which will follow no matter what may be the nuclear strength on our side of the conflict.
The danger of relying too much on the strategic nuclear deterrent is, of course, profoundly true. This is the very reason the North Atlantic Treaty Organization agreed in 1957 to build up its own tactical nuclear deterrent as a supplement to and a backing for that deterrent which can be supplied by conventional forces alone. In the face of overwhelming conventional strength on the other side of the iron curtain, and in the face of the inability of the NATO members at that time and their continuing inability to build up enough conventional divisions to give them the kind of security which they desired and to provide the kind of tactical conventional deterrent that would be useful, the alliance decided to build up a tactical nuclear deterrent to avoid the awful results of having to
Appointment of Defence Committee use the strategic deterrent as the reply to every attack that might be made against Europe or against the alliance.
If the only reply to an assault against western Europe, which might not be general in character and might not even be nuclear in character but which would be overwhelming against smaller armies defending against the attack, was to bring the United States and to a lesser extent the United Kingdom strategic nuclear deterrent into action, that would mean that every assault, however limited it might have been at the beginning, would become the first and last world nuclear war.
This is the justification for the north Atlantic alliance building up a tactical defensive nuclear deterrent. But I would go further than that, and I think the leader of the New Democratic party mentioned this too. It would be even better if NATO had a conventional shield, a conventional deterrent on which it could rely without having to use any kind of nuclear weapons in case of certain types of limited attack; a conventional deterrent, a conventional shield which would be strong enough to hold the line until it became clear whether an all-out assault was under way and the NATO council would have a chance to decide what kind of reply was then needed to meet this attack as it unfolded.
In other words the ideal strategy, of course, for NATO-and Canada takes part in the determination of this strategy-is a conventional shield, a tactical deterrent behind that conventional shield, and then only as a last resort-and it would be a resort which would be an admission of the tragedy of world nuclear war

reliance on the strategic nuclear deterrent which should be limited to those countries that now possess it, the United States of America and to a smaller extent the United Kingdom. That is why that at the recent NATO council meeting and indeed before then NATO has been and is now preoccupied in trying to establish a satisfactory balance between the nuclear and conventional capabilities of the alliance. That is why we in this government, as in other governments in NATO, are particularly concerned at this time when we have so much nuclear strategic power to build up the conventional strength of the alliance. The prime minister seemed to get very excited indeed yesterday-
Oh, oh.

The ex-prime minister. He got very excited indeed over the reply I made to a question yesterday, and I am unable to determine the reason for his excitement. What I said, and I am glad to repeat it and put it on the record again, was that

Appointment of Defence Committee our position-this is the position that was referred to in the NATO communique and agreed upon by all members of the NATO council-is to emphasize the importance of the conventional defences of NATO. There is nothing very surprising about that. It remains the policy of the government to emphasize the importance of the conventional defences of NATO. It is a policy which does not conflict in any way, as I hope to point out, with the carrying out of the obligations, undertakings, pledges, commitments which were made by the previous government. It will be very simple indeed to prove that these commitments were made, and I will come to that a little later. In a speech which I made in January at Scarborough and to which a good deal of attention has been given, because it has often been quoted, I had this to say:
The government should re-examine at once the whole basis of Canadian defence policy. In particular, it should discuss with the United States and with NATO a role for Canada in continental and collective defence which would be more realistic and effective for Canada than the present one. This examination would be concerned, among other things, with the necessity of building up NATO's conventional forces and the part Canada could play in this. However, until the present role is changed-
And this is the role undertaken for Canada by the previous government and bequeathed to us, and it is a nuclear role with certain responsibilities.
-a new Liberal government would put Canada's armed services in the position to discharge fully commitments undertaken for Canada by its predecessor. This would be the only honourable course for any government representing the Canadian people. We would not betray our trust, or weaken Canada's reputation for living up to its word.
The Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, saw fit to make certain statements about the work of the recent NATO council meeting which in my view completely misrepresented both the purposes and the results of that meeting. I am sorry, indeed, that a man who only recently was the head of this government would make some of the remarks he made about the NATO council meeting and about the decisions taken as he saw them at that meeting.
I am sorry also, Mr. Speaker, that he did not see fit to take advantage of the opportunity yesterday when he was speaking-and his remarks roamed far and wide but nobody complained about that-to apologize for the use in this house by one of his colleagues, and a member of the privy council, of a document which is forged; which insulted the United States ambassador to Canada, a document which was designed obviously to poison the relationships between our two countries. It was given additional circulation
IMr. Pearson.]

by the fact that it was produced and cited in this house by my hon. friend, a former minister of the crown. It was unfortunate the Leader of the Opposition could not have cleared up that matter at that time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in order to support the position he took concerning the council meeting and the alleged Canadian position on defence as established at that meeting, the prime minister relied almost entirely on two sources.
Oh, oh.

-I mean the ex-prime minister relied on two sources of information. The first one was the president of the exchequer court, Mr. Justice Thorson, and the other was the Toronto Star. These are two very unusual sources of information for my right hon. friend to rely upon, but they were the ones upon which he relied almost exclusively. He even went so far as to refer to Mr. Justice Thorson as being close to the Liberal party, and that therefore it was possible for this house to accept the statement made by Mr. Justice Thorson as representing the views of the Liberal party on defence matters. Nothing could be further removed from the views of this government than the views on defence matters contained in some of the statements made by Mr. Justice Thorson in the speech from which the right hon. gentleman quoted with such great approval and which he used as the basis for his case to such a large extent. I should like to point out that this gentleman had a right to say these things, although there has been some questioning of the propriety in view of the position he holds.
I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman whether he supports this statement in the speech that he quoted with such great approval:
Certainly, the Canadian people did not give the Liberal government a clear mandate to acquire nuclear warheads for our Bomarcs, nuclear missiles for our Voodoo interceptors, nuclear warheads for our Honest John rockets and hydrogen bombs-[DOT]
That is what they were called by the right hon. gentleman, hydrogen bombs. I will have something to say concerning that a little later.
-for our Starfighters or to join the United States-[DOT]
This is the part to which I take strong exception. I hope the right hon. gentleman does not support this.
-or to join the United States in the madness of the nuclear arms race which it started-
The United States started.
-soon after it dropped its atom bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki early in August of 1945 and killed approximately 150,000 defenceless Japanese civilians and injured as many more.
It is true.

Some hon. gentlemen opposite say that is true, the United States started the nuclear race. Nothing could be said that would .give greater aid and comfort to those whom we consider to be the main threat to peace in the world than a statement of that kind. It is demonstrably false. I remember very well, because I was in Washington at the time and because I took part in the discussions and negotiations later at the United Nations, that the United States government of that day, which was the sole possessor of atomic power for military purposes-nobody else had it- was willing to give up that power and bring it under international control by an arrangement at the United Nations known as the Baruch plan. At the time the United States made this offer to give up this power, to bring it under international control, nobody else had it. This proposal was turned down by the communist bloc, by the Soviet union. I regret very much that a prominent Canadian would make a statement that the United States started the madness of the nuclear arms race. I regret very much indeed that hon. gentlemen opposite have supported that statement.
Since that time all governments that believe in peace and freedom, all governments, have been attempting to bring about an international agreement which would end this nuclear arms race. No government and no country has worked harder in that regard than Canada. I pay my tribute to what the previous government attempted to do in connection with this matter, especially through the work of the former secretary of state for external affairs. The necessity for this kind of international agreement would not have existed if the United States offer in 1945 had been accepted when the United States then had nuclear power. It is regrettable indeed that this kind of talk should be given circulation in Canada.
I want to come now to a question that the Leader of the Opposition dwelt upon at some length and with some vigour. What was the role undertaken by the previous Canadian government in the field of defence? What were the commitments? What were the undertakings? What were the pledges given to our allies as to what we would do in the alliance? It has been suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, and repeated by the Leader of the Opposition last night, that somehow or other at the NATO council meeting a few weeks ago our role was changed and we became a nuclear power by a decision made before that council meeting was held, a decision which was ratified at the council meeting. There is not a word of truth in any such suggestion, Mr. Speaker.
Appointment of Defence Committee
A great deal was said by the right hon. gentleman last night about the nuclear force that was set up at the NATO council meeting. He wanted to know whether Canada was taking part in this, and he also wanted to know whether Canada was going to take part in the other proposed multilateral nuclear force. I hope to satisfy his legitimate curiosity on these matters.
He also criticized us because he said we should never have taken a decision as a government, or indeed as a party before we became a government, in regard to these matters, because it was clear the NATO council meeting in Ottawa would make decisions that would affect Canada's role; and the reason his government held off taking any decision was that it knew the NATO council was going to meet here and it was waiting to see what would be decided at that meeting.
Of course it was perfectly clear to anybody who knew anything about how the NATO council operates-and my own views on this matter have been confirmed by what I have found out since taking office-that nothing would be discussed, let alone decided, at the council meeting here in Ottawa that would affect in any way the role of Canadian forces in NATO, the role undertaken for them by the previous government. To use the NATO council meeting as a smokescreen for the purpose of avoiding the necessity to make any decision, and especially to do this during an election campaign, was just nonsense.
This was just to help the right hon. gentleman avoid the issue. There was no basis of realism about it at all because, as we have learned from what happened at the NATO council meeting, the only things discussed there apart from the decision to re-examine the whole basis of NATO strategy-which will take a long time, and I hope will go hand in hand with our re-examining Canada's strategy in the committee we are talking about-apart from this and the exchange of views on foreign affairs which takes place at every council meeting, the only matters brought up were the possibility of collecting the nuclear forces which had been already committed to NATO-and the Canadian air division was considered as being included in those by all the people who took part in the council discussions, including the secretary general-under a separate NATO command rather than letting them remain under the existing SACEUR command. The question of whether any other forces should be assigned to the new NATO nuclear command if it were set up was also considered.
That has nothing to do with the role undertaken by the Canadian government back in

Appointment of Defence Committee 1959 lor our air division, a role which was undertaken with the knowledge of our allies, a role which was undertaken by the cabinet of that day, a role which could not be carried out without the use of nuclear warheads for the weapons systems which were to be secured, a role which required our aircraft to carry nuclear ammunition, and which the government of the day knew required them to carry that ammunition.

May I ask the Prime Minister this: If there was such a commitment, why did he and those associated with him forever say we should not have entered into such an arrangement and should try to get out of it?
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman is now contradicting himself.
No, I am not contradicting myself. The Prime Minister is contradicting himself.

"If we entered into such a commitment why did the hon. gentleman and his friends not try to get out of it in time"? That is exactly what we tried to do, to advise the government before it was too late not to spend a billion dollars of the taxpayers' money on these weapons systems which were inactive without nuclear warheads.
Is the Prime Minister saying if there was a commitment he was a party to asking us to break that commitment?

Indeed I was a party at the time to that when the commitment was under discussion; and before the equipment was secured I was a party to advising the government to negotiate themselves out of this role and get a better one for Canada. But they refused even to listen to our arguments.
Mr. Speaker, now-
Of course the right hon. gentleman-
I hate to interrupt.
Sit down.
Now, as the right hon. gentleman is becoming so confidential, will he tell why he turned that somersault on January 12?

I will be glad to do that. The right hon. gentleman spoke for about an hour and a quarter last night telling how I turned a somersault. The house is very well informed by him on this matter, but the right hon. gentleman now says there was no commitment, no undertaking, no pledge; I hope my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, who says somebody must be deceiving somebody on this matter, will soon be satisfied.


The truth on this matter is very simple to find, and it was stated in very simple terms by the then minister of national defence, Mr. Pearkes, in 1960. If anybody wants to know about the undertakings made by the Canadian government, the pledges that were given, the commitments that were accepted and the role that was undertaken, they can read what was said by the minister of defence of that time and the minister of defence in the previous government who took his place. I propose to quote from both of them to prove that we were right and accurate in the statements we have made in regard to the undertakings, the pledges given and the commitments accepted by the previous government.
Let me quote first from the then minister of national defence on June 3, 1960, as he spoke during the committee hearings of that day, as recorded at page 230 of the defence expenditures committee proceedings:
At NATO's request-
Not at the request of the parliament of Canada.
At NATO's request the government has recently decided to re-equip the eight squadrons now armed with F-86 Sabre aircraft with an aircraft capable of carrying out a strike reconnaissance role. The aircraft selected for this is the CF-104 ... This aircraft could be armed with a tactical nuclear weapon.
-a weapon referred to as a baby bomb.
Who referred to it as a baby bomb?
It was referred to as a baby bomb, and the government accepted that reference.
Who referred to it as that?
The hon. member for Trinity.
Oh, the baby minister.

And my right hon. friend, four years later, last night called it a baby bomb. Later on during the committee proceedings Mr. Pearkes said this, talking about the new strike reconnaissance role and the aircraft for that role:
It is well known then that the CF-104 would have weapons which would have or could have a nuclear capability.
Mr. Hellyer then said:
The minister said it is well known. Can he state any evidence prior to his announcement of the matter that the CF-104 would be used in a bomb carrying role?
Mr. Pearkes replied:
You were well aware of it.
Mr. Speaker, even we were supposed to be well aware of it, but now the former government says it was not aware of it.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, at the luncheon recess I was dealing with the point made by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition yesterday that somehow, in some way, the Canadian government undertook at the recent NATO council meeting a new nuclear role for Canadian forces in NATO, particularly for the Canadian air division in Europe. He made some reference to that new role, which I will quote later. But I showed, from the evidence of the minister of national defence himself as far back as 1960, that this particular strike reconnaissance role was undertaken by the Canadian government of that day and that the Canadian forces were committed to that role. I showed from that evidence that this role could not be performed except by the acquisition of nuclear ammunition for the weapons systems which were to be acquired for it, and that this was understood by the government of the day and indeed by the allies with whom we worked in NATO, for whom, as well as for ourselves, this role was accepted. Indeed, at that time before the committee on July 11, 1960, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) asked the minister of national defence:
Will the Canadian government have a say as to whether atomic weapons carried by the CF-104 can be used or will this be a power and authority held in the control of others?
The then minister of national defence, Mr. Pearkes, said:
They would be used if and when they are required.
Then he went on to say:
Those details in connection with the use or storage of these weapons in Europe depend upon a note which has not yet been completed.
Indeed, it was not completed by the time the Conservative government went out of office, but there was no doubt in anybody's mind as to the role undertaken and the only way in which that role could be discharged. When the right hon. the Leader of the Opposition talks about some nuclear offensive or aggressive role having been undertaken by this government, for example, he must have known that the role to be performed by the R.C.A.F. air division in Europe is the same role that was undertaken for it by the previous government. Mr. Pearkes, his minister of national defence, described in detail at the time what that role was and what was involved in it. There is the undertaking, the pledge and the commitment.
I quote from page 502 of the report of the special committee on defence expenditures
Appointment of Defence Committee on July 11, 1960 when Mr. Pearkes, the minister, was asked what this role would be. He was asked the specific question by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and his reply was:
To intercept enemy bombers; while the CF-104 is, as I have said, a strike reconnaissance aircraft, one which is to be used for reconnaissance purposes, and one which is to be used against ground targets. It is not an air defence weapon, with the idea of attacking enemy bombers, and it would not come into use until the enemy was actually on the move.
Nothing could state more clearly the role of the air division as it was undertaken at that time. That, again I repeat, was the commitment which was accepted. As reported at page 327 of this committee report Mr. Pearkes had something to say about this on June 22:
I do not see how I can go any further than the statement made by the Prime Minister on January 18 when he said that eventually the Canadian forces will require certain nuclear weapons, if the Canadian forces are to be kept effective. This will be done by placing the nuclear warheads in the Bomarcs, into the aircraft missiles.
What could be clearer than that in regard to a commitment undertaken by the Canadian government:
This will be done by placing the nuclear warheads in the Bomarcs, into the aircraft missiles. To be effective eventually the Canadian forces will have to be equipped with nuclear warheads.
To try to slip out of this undertaking, this commitment, by arguing that there was no formal treaty, no formal arrangement, nothing signed, is merely playing with words; playing with the word "commitment" if you like. If there ever was an undertaking by a Canadian government and accepted as such by our allies, who transferred this particular role to the Canadian forces-and if they had not taken it on, one of our allies would have had to take it on-this is it. But the fact is that the government, having taken on that role, refused to take on the means to discharge the role. To say now that it would have been possible in an emergency, in the awful emergency of war, to have followed through at that time and accepted the ammunition to go with the warheads, is an affront to anyone's intelligence. To say that the Canadian air division, having accepted a role which required a certain type of ammunition for its weapons systems, which ammunition could only be acquired after a political agreement made with the country, the United States, which manufactured the ammunition, and to say that this agreement could have been reached and the ammunition supplied after the emergency developed, after the war began, is childish in the extreme. Yet that is the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite. It is not the position taken

Appointment of Defence Committee by the two hon. gentlemen who were ministers of national defence in that government. Indeed, it is not the position taken by hon. gentlemen who left that government because they could not accept the defence policy of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. If any ministers must have known what was going on and the extent of the obligations we undertook, surely it would be the ministers of national defence. I have already quoted what the minister of national defence, Mr. Pearkes, said in 1960. The minister of national defence who took his place, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) was quite specific about this the other night when speaking in this house. I quote from page 643 of Hansard, where the hon. member had this to say:
At the present time, the Liberals have adopted this policy-
That is, the policy of the government when he was minister of national defence:
-in its entirety, so far as one can see. I believe that they should be honest and say that they have adopted the Conservative defence policies of the last five years instead of trying to pin their position to the narrow ground of merely living up to commitments made by the previous government.
But this is exactly the position which the Leader of the Opposition flatly refuses to accept. These may be the policies, in the mind of the then minister of national defence -and, indeed, they are the correct policies- but they are absolutely denied by his own leader and are contrary to the statements made by his leader. So we might well ask ourselves, where is the truth in this matter? The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer then asked the hon. member:
In his opinion

That is, in the opinion of the hon. gentleman:
-was the previous government committed to the acquisition of nuclear warheads for use in some *of the weapons systems it had acquired?
The hon. member for Calgary North answered:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that the acquisition of these four weapons systems indicated an intention on the part of the government to supply them the ammunition which would make them effective.
How can anyone believe that a government would spend nearly a billion dollars on weapons systems and then refuse to accept the ammunition which alone would make the weapons systems effective? The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness), according to the Winnipeg Free Press of yesterday-and I quote from it-had an interview with the correspondent of that paper in Ottawa, dated Ottawa, June 6, and here is the report of that interview. This is from yesterday's Winnipeg Free Press, by Vic Mackie:

The Hon. Douglas Harkness, former minister of defence, told the Free Press today that "documents exist setting out Canada's obligations" to acquire nuclear weapons for Canadian forces.
And if anyone should know, the former minister should know-and the former minister will be given an opportunity, when he is a member of this committee, to bring forward all the information which he appropriately can in connection with this matter. The hon. gentleman went on to say in this interview-I shall continue to read the report:
"The obligations are there." He acknowledged that some people termed them "commitments" and added that it all depended upon how you interpreted the word "commitments".
He then went on to say:
"But there is no question in my mind that the documents do exist and can be produced. They contain certain obligations or commitments."
This is the former minister of national defence. They contain, he said, certain obligations or commitments-
May I ask the Prime Minister if he will produce those documents?

If those documents contain classified information, and if their production will be prejudicial to the security of this country, they will be refused. If they are not, they will not be refused.
The former minister of defence went on to say:
Whether they should be produced is another question. He stressed, in an exclusive interview in his west block office, that the documents are "classified" and cannot be tabled in the house for security reasons.
Again, this is the former minister speaking.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this throws quite enough light, and from a source not on this side of the house but on the other side of the house, to enable us to see whether there was an obligation, or an undertaking, or a pledge in this respect. Surely it shows beyond possibility of doubt that the role which was undertaken in 1959-60 for the air division is the role which the division is being asked to perform at this time, in June, 1963; and for the Leader of the Opposition, basing his authority on a statement of a justice of the Exchequer Court of Canada, to give the impression that the NATO council is, somehow, imposing on the Canadian air division a new role, is deceitful nonsense.
Here is what the right hon. gentleman had to say about this new role, as he termed it, undertaken by Canadian forces. I quote from yesterday's Hansard. Having referred to Mr. Justice Thorson and quoted with approval from his speech, the right hon. gentleman went on to say:

Then, even before the NATO meetings, the Canadian government had capitulated to the extent that these tactical forces in Europe were being equipped with offensive weapons.
The right hon. gentleman made an accusation yesterday, in those words, that the Canadian air division in NATO is now being equipped with offensive weapons. Mr. Speaker, they are being equipped with the weapons secured for them by the right hon. gentleman.
Nothing of the kind.

Then he went on to say this, as will be found quoted on page 751:
These are things we would like to know. Canada has become involved first of all in providing this tremendous power to NATO through our air force Starfighters, actually an aggressive nuclear force far and beyond what is contemplated by the expression "defensive weapons''.
The former prime minister of this country has termed the course to which our air division is committed under NATO, a defensive alliance, as being an aggressive nuclear force.
Does the Prime Minister say that a million ton explosive bomb is a defensive instrument? It is nothing of the kind.

If that force is used to defend us against an attack or defend us after an attack-and that is the only way in which Canadian forces would ever be used under NATO-then it is a defensive weapon. I think it is shameful for the Leader of the Opposition to refer to a Canadian element of the NATO defensive forces as an aggressive nuclear force.
Then the right hon. gentleman asked me some questions about another allied nuclear force which he claims to have been set up by the NATO council and of which he argues the Canadian air division is now part. He also wished to get some information about the other collective force, the multilateral nuclear force. The Leader of the Opposition has read the NATO communique and he must know that no such inter-allied nuclear force was set up by the NATO council. There was discussion of the possibility of an inter-allied nuclear force, and this is referred to in the communique, in paragraph 8, as follows:
The ministers discussed NATO defence policy and approved the steps taken to organize the nuclear forces assigned or to be assigned to the supreme allied commander, Europe.
This means that if we have an air division in Europe which has been assigned a role by the previous government in agreement with NATO, a role which cannot be discharged without these particular weapons, it seems to me to be entirely a problem of organization whether that force should be under a separate NATO command or under
7, 1963
Appointment of Defence Committee the supreme commander, Europe. That is the only thing involved in these discussions and no decision was made at the time in respect to it. The matter is still under consideration.
I must say, too, that as long as we are undertaking this role-and we shall be reexamining this role ourselves in the next few months-let us discharge it as efficiently as we can.
The right hon. gentleman had some satirical observations to make about the multilateral nuclear force. I do not know whether he considers this to be an aggressive nuclear force. He had suspicions about Mr. Livingston Merchant, a former United States ambassador to Ottawa who was admired as an ambassador by most Canadians who knew him. He asked me to tell him, in the house, all about the multilateral nuclear force. He even asked me what changes the United States government plans to make to the McMahon act in order to help to bring this force into being,
Would that not be a subject of discussion?

Of course it would, but the right hon. gentleman asked me to stand up and say in this House of Commons what changes the United States government intends' to make through congress. If and when it is-set up, this would be an organizational development under NATO to which might be added United Kingdom bomber force and, perhaps, United States submarines. But it would be under NATO organizational command.
The multilateral nuclear force is something else. It is a mixed force of surface ships with nuclear weapons, and those ships would be manned by representatives of more than one nation under a multilateral command. That is the proposal which is being discussed. The right hon. gentleman asked me to give details of these matters. The details will have to be worked out if and when the countries of NATO decide to go ahead with this multilateral nuclear force. The Leader of the Opposition expressed impatience about not knowing much about it, yet he told us last night this proposal was put forward in Nassau in the Bahamas. And when he came back from Nassau he did not tell us anything about it at all.
Mr. Speaker, may I say to the hon. gentleman that apparently he does not agree that there was a communique issued which set out that fact? Of course, I realize he did not read it.

I read the communique, Mr. Speaker, and if the right hon. gentleman is satisfied that all the information this House

Appointment of Defence Committee of Commons requires is in this communique then he absolves me from any responsibility of saying anything more.
That communique was not written before the meeting.

I think I should tell the house a little more than appeared in the Nassau communique. The purpose of this multilateral nuclear force-this is well known; I am not betraying secrets of other governments when I say this-is to build up a collective control and a collective custody of nuclear weapons which would become a nuclear deterrent force at the disposition of the Atlantic alliance. The purpose of this is to discourage, and if possible to prevent, the development of national nuclear forces. It is no secret that when we talk about the discouragement of the development of national nuclear forces we have very much in mind in the Atlantic alliance the discouragement of the development of a German national nuclear force. Therefore it was thought by those who put this proposal forward that a multilateral international force which is under international control and with weapons in international custody might be a development away from the possibility of national nuclear forces, and there is something no doubt to be said for that.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the house, although I do not need to, that Canada has no intention whatever of developing national nuclear forces or of manufacturing national nuclear weapons. While we will give this proposal consideration, as indeed we are bound and are anxious to give consideration to any proposal made to us by any of our NATO allies-and we do not exclude the United States from that group-I do not think that it will be likely that we would wish to add to our existing responsibilities and commitments by participating in this kind of multilateral nuclear force. But this is a matter which will be given the consideration it deserves.
The right hon. gentleman asked me categorically to tell him whether negotiations were going on now about the supply of U.S. warheads for Canadian forces and the supply of nuclear warheads for United States defensive squadrons already established on Canadian soil as a result of an agreement between the two countries, in this case an agreement going back to the leased bases agreement of many years ago. I can tell the right hon. gentleman, as has already been mentioned, that we are reopening negotiations which were begun by my right hon. friend and his government with a view to making the political agreement without which there cannot be a technical arrangement to make possible the acquisition of the ammunition for these weapons systems. So far as negotiations concerning the U.S.

air bases in Canada are concerned, these negotiations began long ago, and were begun by my right hon. friend and his government.
Are they continuing?

If my right hon. friend would bother to look at the proceedings of the special committee on defence expenditures for June 22 and subsequent days he will get all the information about these negotiations-what was proposed, what was hoped for, what was intended. The minister of defence at that time said there was an exchange of notes going on covering that matter. For some reasons those negotiations were broken off suddenly by the previous government and they have not been resumed by the present government.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have dealt with, if not all, at least a good many points raised in this discussion on this resolution to set up a defence committee. I hope the defence committee can be set up without delay. I feel sure it can perform a very useful function in clarifying defence problems and in getting information for members on defence matters. I hope there will be called before that committee defence experts, and I hope as a result of the work of a committee of this kind the government of the day will be assisted in the re-examination which it is giving to our whole defence policy, so that we may be sure, so far as it is possible to be sure in a changing world, that in the future we will accept the right commitments for Canada in the field of defence, and that when we accept them we will be able to discharge them.
Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister accept a question?
Yes.

The Prime Minister, like the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) in his speech, laid very much stress on the so-called commitments, or series of commitments, and went into it at such length that it is obvious that he wanted to lay at the door of the Conservative party the blame for the policy-

A supplementary question. Did not the Minister of National Defence say in his speech that it was necessary that another agreement be signed before we acquired them? Does that not leave room to get out if we do not think it is wise?
