speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the establishment of an economic council of Canada and to define the duties thereof, to provide for the appointment of the chairman, directors and other members of the council and for the payment of the remuneration of the chairman and directors and of certain other expenses of administration of the council, to provide further that the council may engage the services of such advisers and staff as may be necessary to enable it to carry out its duties and to provide further for other related and incidental matters.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution you have just read states that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the establishment of an economic council of Canada and to define the duties thereof, and it goes on to give certain other details in connection with the work of the council. My purpose in the brief remarks I am making today on the resolution is to outline in broad terms and clearly, I hope, the government's purpose in the legislation which it asks leave to introduce into the house. Obviously a more detailed discussion of the structure and the operation which we propose for the economic council of Canada cannot take place until the bill itself is before the house. This resolution, I hope, will clear the way for that purpose. Our intention, if the house agrees, is to proceed promptly to the further and more detailed stage of parliamentary discussion with a bill before the house.
The idea embodied in the resolution is one to which I believe all parties in the house agree in principle, or agreed in principle at least in the last parliament. So far as this government is concerned, the resolution embodies an idea that goes back for us more than five years to the policies which the Liberal party adopted and put forward at the beginning of 1958 in regard to economic planning, which policies, Mr. Chairman, when they were put forward as they were in the house in the form of resolutions, were summarily rejected by the government of that day.

Economic Council of Canada
Our proposals at that time were prompted by an awareness that the economic problems and the economic needs of Canada were changing with changing circumstances. Indeed, the likelihood of such a change had been anticipated some years earlier by the government of that day when it established a royal commission on Canada's economic prospects under the chairmanship of my colleague, the present Minister of Finance.
In 1958 we were aware also and have become more aware since that other countries, particularly the European countries which faced such appalling problems of reconstruction and economic development after the war, had created and were creating new instruments to help in economic policy planning and economic policy making. The economic progress since achieved in western Europe has brought these developments very widely to the public attention and they are often summed up in the one word, planning.
Though the planning that was introduced into the western European countries after world war II varied, of course, in different countries, within the past few years planning has become almost a fashionable word even in some quarters where traditionally there has been a good deal of reserve about any extension of the role of government in our economy. I remember from reading my history that away back in the late 1880's, I think it was, in Great Britain Sir William Harcourt, who was then chancellor of the exchequer, I believe, in commenting on the growth of popular education and referring specifically to the last of the great education bills of that particular century, as well as commenting on the fact that the very first sort of rudimentary stages of social security legislation had been introduced into the British House of Commons toward the end of the century, said "we are all socialists now" on the strength of that development.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, it is a little more accurate to say, in respect of what has been happening in recent years, that we are all planners now, though the concept of planning is not the same in all cases. I, myself, think that planning, far from being a word to arouse suspicion, is a very good word indeed. However, it has to be used with a certain amount of caution; that is to say, it is a good word, provided that when we use it we know what we mean by it. We must not fall into the trap, in my view, of thinking that something called planning is, itself, a magic key to economic progress. It is merely a means to an end.
In Europe, there is no simple correlation between the extent of planning in the various countries and the different rates of economic

growth that those countries have achieved since world war II. In fact, within Europe itself there is a broad range of planning techniques adapted to different economic situations, different constitutional and different political conditions. The French concept of planning, as embodied in their legislation, is really very all-embracing, and the organization of plans in Paris really overshadows most of the government departments in its actions, in its extent and in its complexity. The one country in Europe which has had, perhaps, the most exciting economic progress since the destruction and dislocation of world war II, the federal republic of West Germany, has itself indulged in a minimum of economic planning. It is impossible, therefore, to talk about planning in a generic way because planning itself differs in various European countries who have benefited from it, and other countries have benefited without very much planning at all.
Some of the techniques used in Europe would be alien to our federal constitution in Canada and our kind of economy, yet anyone who read the report of the commission of the productivity council that went to Europe about a year and a half ago could hardly help but be impressed by what has been accomplished in most European countries by the implementation of economic planning,, especially by the emphasis laid in that planning on the use of planning techniques as a method of co-operation between capital, labour and government. There are, and I have mentioned some of them, important reservations. Yet, with these reservations, it is still true that there is much we can usefully learn from the experience of European countries.
The basic thing I believe, Mr. Chairman, the experience that is common in the various countries, is that all the countries where the planning has been instituted have all succeeded in establishing by consultation between government and the public in its varying manifestation of public activity, a broad consensus about the objectives and methods of economic policy and broad agreement on the targets and goals which should be achieved by economic activity. The government's hope, Mr. Chairman, is that we can establish an economic council of Canada which will be an effective instrument for creating in Canada this kind of economic consensus, the kind of economic understanding that we need if we are to make the most of our resources, achieve and maintain high levels of employment, make our economic growth adequate for that purpose and compete successfully, as we must, in the new trading world.

The essential purpose of the council, as we see it, will be objectively to appraise economic trends, to assess economic problems, and so on. This appraisal must not, of course, be made in vacuo, if I may use that phrase, but must be made to serve as a basis for sound policy decisions by government, by business, by labour and by other economic groups. In other words, if planning in government or planning between government and private organizations or agencies outside government is to be effective, it has got to be more than merely an academic exercise.
When the economy has been studied as a whole, when its prospects and its potential have been assessed, the need which has been recognized in most of the free economies of the world is to relate these general prospects, and these general needs, to the particular plans of individual industries and of government agencies at all levels, and bring these together so that each will know what the other is proposing and hopes to do. Our great corporations, our provincial governments, our public agencies-they already plan. Where major investment projects costing tens of millions of dollars are involved, such planning is done many years ahead. But at present, all this partial planning within our economy is not related; it is not co-ordinated. Much of it is done without knowledge of what is intended by other corporations, other agencies or by government agencies. This is one thing that a central planning agency, a central planning council of the kind that is referred to in this resolution will be able to do. It will be able to co-ordinate all the planning that goes on in our economy. It might even be able to avoid the proliferation of planning.
The great value, as we see it, of the economic council will lie in bringing together the thinking of government and the thinking of our great industries, our trade unions, our farm organizations, so that they can together take an understanding and far-sighted view of the policy needs that exist in the private sphere, just as much as in the public sphere of our national life. A vital part of the work visualized in this kind of council, this kind of planning, is to develop and deepen cooperation between management and labour, in so far as government has their responsibility in that field.
Now, all this cannot be done by vague talk about planning or by dealing in vague generalities. It means that the proposed council, and the representatives of the major sectors of our economy, labour, capital and government, must be able to sit down together and freely discuss, with representatives of their own choice, how they see the prospects and
Economic Council of Canada the needs of each sector of the economy, and how the needs of one sector apply to the needs of the other. The government's bill is intended to provide for that sort of planning.
In doing so, it will meet the deficiencies to which spokesmen for the Liberal party drew attention in the bill that was before the last parliament. It will also, I think, meet some of the criticisms levelled at the previous government's bill on behalf of the New Democratic party. At the same time, I want to make it clear to the New Democratic party that when we talk about planning, on this side, we are not joining the people who talk about setting up a planned economy in the sense of an all-embracing, far reaching, rigid government regulation over business and labour, which involves controls, quotas and prohibitions which are designed to replace the ordinary operation of our business system. In wartime, of course, we have had to have that kind of planned economy, but anyone who thinks that Canada could be run that way in peacetime is, 1 believe, simply dreaming and is not in accord with the realities of our situation.
I would ask the New Democratic party, whatever theoretical preferences they may have, whether a planned economy of that kind could possibly work in Canada? Could it win the acceptance-without which, of course it could not work-and the co-operation of ordinary people that all efficient government policies have to have in order to make them work? Could it do that except in time of great national emergency or the greatest national emergency of all, which is the condition of war? I believe it could not.
Mr. Chairman, the concern of the government is with what is possible and urgently desirable and not with what is perhaps theoretically attractive, but which results in ordering people around unnecessarily. What is possible, and needed, is more care, more consultation and more foresight in making decisions, public and private. A modem government has enormous influence on the circumstances that shape private decisions, and it should use that influence to the advantage of the nation and the welfare of its people. A modern government needs to know where the thinking of business, labour and other groups is pointing. Planning, as we mean it, means consultation in order to replace haphazard influence by conscious guidance. It means both government policies and private policies will be more broad-based and long-sighted than at present.
I think I may claim the purposes of an economic council, as we intend them in this proposed legislation, were set out some time ago in a leaflet published by the Liberal party early in 1962. A passage from this

Economic Council of Canada leaflet was quoted by one of my colleagues in the last parliament, but I think it is appropriate that I quote it again at the beginning of our discussions on this resolution and on the bill which will follow it.
Our party committed itself in that pamphlet as follows:
Nations and governments now face economic problems, both at home and abroad, even more complex than those of the early years after the war.
The economic advisory council-
-which we are proposing now should be called the economic council of Canada-
-will be the means to bring foresight consistently and systematically to bear on our national problems.
The council's members will have a wide variety of experience in business, in labour matters, in farming, in government and in public enterprises. They must be assisted by expert staff.
The council's function will be to know, by direct contact, what is going on and what is planned in all types of industry and all regions of Canada. It will investigate economic trends, promote research, study such major problems as the impact of automation on industry and on the individual. It will bring information and study into focus for the guidance not only of government but also of all private organizations.
The council will publish outlook reports. It will suggest practical economic targets, so that the federal government, the municipalities and private organizations can together take a reasoned view of our economic needs and the policies required to meet those needs.
Government will then know where the thinking of business and labour and other groups is pointing. They, in turn, will better know the direction of the government policies that so much influence business conditions. They will know what Ottawa is aiming at, and can make their own plans with foresight. Both government policies and private policies will be based on clearer knowledge of what is going on, on better understanding and a longer view.
Some hon. members opposite have voiced what is to me a somewhat strange apprehension that this government may abdicate responsibility by setting up a variety of boards and councils to govern for it. I do not think I really need to say that they should have no such fears. Neither this council nor any other agency which we may be setting up will replace the responsibility of government in a democratic and representative parliament. No government could, I believe, have made it clearer, and we will continue to make it clear, that this government accepts wholeheartedly full responsibility to parliament for decisions on national economic policy.
Where we perhaps differ from our predecessors is that we are determined to make these decisions on full information and with the assistance of modern machinery to help us in policy making. That is the purpose of our legislation. It is the purpose of a government determined to do its job to the best of its ability; not more than the job

which is the proper responsibility of the federal government, but all of that job.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have followed with care the remarks of the Prime Minister. I was very much interested in the document from which he read, dealing with the duties of government and the aversion of himself, and those associated with him, to accepting the principle that boards and the like should take the place of government. If he meant what he said it certainly shows that time does educate for he, and many of those seated around him, were the people who in the days of war, when it was excusable, and then after the war until 1957, believed in the principle that it was perfectly proper to push people around. That was their attitude. That was a major part of their activities, and I am more than pleased to hear the Prime Minister say that attitude will no longer be followed by him and those associated with him.
I could not help but smile when he hearkened back to the days of Sir William Har-court, and quoted that eminent British statesman as having stated "We are all socialists now." The government today in economic matters suffers from cabinet schizophrenia.
Then there are the planners, the men who in the days of the war and afterwards pushed Canada around; the men who believed that there should be no right to appeal against autocratic orders, that the individual should not be able to go to the courts. And paid. Well, when you are pushing people around you do not mind paying somebody for doing it; that is their view. But what is the meaning of "directors"? We will have to wait and see. All we have to say is that the general principle, if after careful examination it is in effect a prototype of the legislation which we introduced, will receive our support. But if the addition of the words with regard to the appointment of directors means the acceptance of directive planning, then we shall certainly have to give the fullest consideration to the course we will take. Certainly the distinction drawn by the Prime Minister is appropriate. Today planing is done, and must be done, in every field of endeavour. But government cannot go beyond the ambit of indicative planning. That is our stand and we are very definite in that regard.
We await the introduction of the bill, because if these directors are to have the powers that directors normally have, then we want to say to the government that we in this party are opposed to any agency or device which will provide bureaucratic control over the business life of Canada. I think the Prime Minister had some of these ideas in mind because he rather laboured when he tried to explain that this was just a board similar to the one that was accepted in principle last November, December and January. On the other hand, in every part of this country today businessmen are beginning to worry. Business has a right to be required to consider the welfare of the state at all times. We will never build up the kind of economic growth in Canada that each of us hopes for, ever expanding, on the basis of control whereby one, two, three or four theoretical economists, knowing in their own minds what is good for everyone, will be placed in a position to enforce their theories.
I would point out in this connection that the president of the Royal Bank of Canada spoke the other day on this question. He is very much concerned with the question of economic planning. He said:
Planning once begun tends to feed on itself. The dislocations which inevitably occur become the excuse for further plans on an ever more grandiose scale.
As I said a moment ago, we intend to support this resolution because we want to see the bill. We intend to examine it carefully, but we do not intend to follow the course that hon. gentlemen opposite followed last fall and January, when they gave vocal support to legislation which they believed was necessary and which was acceptable to them, while at the same time doing everything they could to prevent that beneficial legislation being brought into effect.

Economic Council of Canada
So far as directional planning is concerned, no doubt we will be able to get some information on this once we see the bill itself. Under this directional planning will it be the objective that Canada's percentage of growth in 1963 shall exceed that of 1962? You will remember, sir, that during the election campaign and even before those opposite said that Canada's economy was failing, that it was deteriorating, that all was economic ruin in this nation. Yet when at the conclusion of the year objective statistics were secured, it was seen that Canada had the largest percentage of economic growth of any country in the world. It amounted to some 8 per cent. Making allowance for the difference in inflationary trends, it represented an increase in volume of not very much less than 8 per cent. I repeat, it was the largest percentage of economic growth of any major country in the world. We shall be glad to hear what the government has in mind in this regard. Nothing has been said about this since hon. gentlemen took their seats on the other side of the chamber. Are they going to increase this year the rate of growth which took place in the last year of our party's administration? I think, Mr. Chairman, that the reason they have said nothing about it is that they realize it is going to be next to impossible to equal the economic progress which was made by the Conservative government during the period of its administration.
In the second place, we have not heard very much about unemployment. Strangely, it is a word which is not used around here any more. Over and over again, day in and day out for the last several years, we have heard about unemployment. When we succeeded in reducing that unemployment rate there was chagrin in the hearts and minds of those who sit opposite. We believe that as a result of the policies which we initiated, and which were ridiculed, the pegging of the dollar, and the other measures which we took to bring about incentives for production, the number of those unemployed by this summer would be relatively small and that we would be able to hold down the unemployment percentage which has existed in the last couple of years-no higher in Canada by comparison than in the United States, having regard to different climatic conditions. But we have not heard anything about that.
I should like to know from those who bring this matter before the house what are the economic objectives for unemployment for 1963 and 1964. Oh, these 60 days of decision, in the light of experience of the last few weeks have become 60 days of mirage. I remember the mirage so well in the old days :in western Canada. A traveller would see in

the distance castles in the air, only to find later that they were non-existent. That mirage which was brought before the eyes of the Canadian people a few short months ago, the promise of the tremendous expansion which would take place under this new government, will prove no more substantial.
I would ask members opposite to let us know what they have in mind as a suitable increase in the gross national product for this year and next year and, on the basis of their experience since they have taken office, what they have in mind with regard to the reduction of unemployment during 1963 and 1964. These mirages have been brought before us over and over again. What will happen? We are near the three quarter mark in the 60 days of decision and we have heard nothing about those two problems yet.
Reference has been made to planning boards in other parts of the world-in France and in Britain. All of this can be discussed properly when we see the bill. Except for the fact, as I said a moment ago, that the word "directors" occupies such a large place in this resolution, the measure is, in effect, a facsimile of that which we introduced and to which members opposite gave their vocal support-a support which did not extend to bringing about the enactment of the legislation. That is not going to be our attitude. Our attitude will be to support those things which we believe are likely to prove beneficial. If we are given some idea of what this planning will involve-and we can only determine that when we see the bill-and if we find it to be indicative of benefit we shall give it our support. But when the Prime Minister said the last government did not have the benefit of the views of outstanding Canadians with regard to the measures we introduced, he was not paying high tribute to the civil service of this country which gave to us at all times, in the highest echelons, the best advice of which it was capable.

I rise at this time to indicate the support of those in this party for the resolution which is now before the committee.
We would much prefer to have had the opportunity to discuss the resolution with regard to the setting up of the municipal development and loan board, because we are convinced that this measure is one of the most important which will be brought before the house in this coming session. The measure now before us takes what might be called a long term view of economic conditions in Canada; it is an attempt to find solutions to the major problems which face us over an extended period. We are convinced that the other measure to which I have referred is

one which could bring immediate benefits to the economy and help to solve many of the problems which face us at the present time.
Be this as it may, we now have before us a resolution preceding the bill to set up an economic council for Canada. We all remember that in the course of the last parliament there was considerable debate on a measure which was very similar to this. I suppose if we were to look back and consider what was said during those debates in the light of what may be said in the course of the present debate, we would find there would probably be considerable repetition. It may be that the two main parties need only to interchange speeches. Nevertheless, we still face the responsibility of considering this resolution.
I was interested to hear the Prime Minister speak at great length when he introduced this resolution of the importance of economic planning. He said the word "planning" had now become almost fashionable in some areas where, previously, it had been frowned upon. He suggested it might now be a good word and was at pains to justify his frequent references to economic planning and the place it should occupy in the thoughts of the Canadian people at the present time. With respect to this, I should like to refer to the words spoken by the leader of our party in the last parliament when he said:
Planning is good. But planning which reaches down from the top defeats the very purpose of a democratic society. Planning that permits people collectively to work together and plan from the grass roots up, is good.
I think that places on record our views with respect to the type of planning which would be acceptable to us at present.
Referring to the position of the New Democratic party, the Prime Minister asked the question whether the type of planning they had in mind could be carried out in time of peace. His thought apparently is, is it possible rather than is it desirable. Perhaps he could clarify that the next time he participates in the discussion. It would be interesting to find out whether in his mind the planning suggested by the socialists is or is not desirable in his thinking.
Reference has been made to the proliferation of planning agencies, and I think this is something we have to keep in mind because we have so many planning agencies and bodies and organizations now, right from the municipal and school board level up through the various levels of the government, the various organizations concerned about the economic conditions of the country. We have so many of these organizations which have given considerable thought and attention to the matter of the economic conditions of and 28902-5-51

I think the suggestion of the Prime Minister is met when he referred to the fact that this would be more in the nature of a co-ordinating body with representatives of various groups interested in this matter, working in co-operation and consultation with a view to establishing the very best program possible for the future development of our country. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that we are agreed that we in Canada have not reached that degree of development and expansion that is possible or desirable. There is no question that we have made headway and progress, but when we consider the matter in the light of the possibilities I suggest we have fallen far short of what we could have attained had this matter been taken in hand carefully, and with determination and vision, with a view to giving guidance and encouragement under the various sectors of our economy.
I suggest we ought to look at the matter of unemployment. This has been referred to in the course of the debate, but I would suggest that it is a paradox in a nation such as ours, with our tremendous resources, productive capacities, with our manpower and skills, that at such a time as this the rate of unemployment could stand as it does. Surely there should be some way of applying the skills and the manpower to the natural resources in order to produce the goods which people require and can use. Therefore I do not think we have anything to be proud about when we consider the level of employment at the present time. I suggest that this is a matter which should receive immediate consideration, and after all the picture has been assessed and the factors considered then perhaps we will go ahead and do something about our unemployment problem. I insist that this is of immediate urgency, because when there are so many of our people unable to find gainful and productive employment it not only works a hardship on them but is a disgrace to the society of which we are a part.

Mr. Chairman, as the Prime Minister pointed out when he introduced the resolution the opportunity for full discussion will come more rationally when the bill is before the house-although for my part I do not think there is very much doubt as to what kind of bill it is going to be, because I recall that last year when the former government introduced a bill along this line they were accused of having stolen the pants off the Liberal party. Presumably, therefore, the Liberal government, now that it is back, will bring in somewhat the same sort of bill. In fact, I rather gathered that from the Prime Minister's warning, shall we say, to members of this party that the bill would not meet our requirements.
In that connection, sir, I would hope that the Prime Minister knows better than his analysis of this party's policy because if he does not it will fill me with dismay to think that the Prime Minister of Canada is so ignorant of political and economic theory as really to hold those views of the policies of this party. He mentioned in the course of his speech how much opposed his government was to the whole concept of governments pushing people around. So are we, but we are also concerned with something else. We are very much concerned with the problem of certain groups of people pushing governments around as they have been pushed around throughout the lifetime of Canada. To my mind in this present age that is the real problem we are facing.
While we do not have the bill before us and cannot discuss what may be expected from it, I think it is worth while at this time to spend a few minutes in outlining what we in this party consider to be some of the major problems that are going to face the government and this economic planning council. First among them I would put the problem of foreign ownership. I know that this problem is one that has concerned at least some members of the government party. I recall that the present Minister of Finance had this to say on October 4, 1962, as found on page 185 of Hansard of that year:

I believe we can stop this sell-out of our natural resources and our Canadian companies. We can buy back in the years to come many of the resources and many of the Canadian companies that are now in foreign hands.
Then he repeated that sentiment later on the 22nd and suggested that there should be steps taken to see that Canadians participate in the development of the industries in question, such as chemicals and petrochemicals. On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, only the other day, on May 28 to be precise, I noted that the Minister of Finance in answer to a question in this chamber said that the government welcomes an increased inflow of foreign capital into the country, which seems a rather extraordinary attitude for him to take when only a few months ago he was warning us of the dangers of increased foreign ownership and control of Canadian industries and resources. It may be, of course, a case of the old adage of when the devil was sick the devil a monk would be, but when the devil was well the devil of a monk was he. In this case, of course, health or ill health is to be connected with political success or failure. Possibly we have a transmutation of ideas of the Minister of Finance since he was elevated to that high position.
In this connection I should like to quote from a very interesting speech made by the president of the Montreal and Canadian stock exchange yesterday in the city of Quebec in which he had this to say, as found in today's Globe and Mail:
The United States gets a remarkably large return in foreign exchange from relatively small amounts of capital invested by its corporations in foreign countries, including Canada. In the case of Canada, U.s. corporations have no intention of selling part of the equity of their Canadian subsidiaries to this country's investing public.
Mr. Kierans said the major source of direct investment flowing into manufacturing is the United States and that 45 per cent of all of this capital has been absorbed by manufacturing industries-
Among the documents he included to illustrate his point was a statement to a U.S. congressional hearing by Eldridge Haynes, president of Business International of New York, on the performance of 32 overseas trading corporations of 21 U.S. manufacturers in 1959-60.
The $10,548,000 total of equity investments from the United States since incorporation produced an inflow of $277,251,000 in the two year period being surveyed. The original capital outlay also generated sufficient funds overseas to permit the investment of $24,008,000 in underdeveloped and developed countries-
Mr. Kierans referred to current talk about the reorganization of industry and planning by investment corporations to buy Canada back. An illuminating document on this was an appendix to the speech dealing with the Montreal stock exchange's two year program designed to encourage U.S. parent companies to sell part of the equity of their Canadian subsidiaries to Canadians. "The response was completely negative," said an introduction to excerpts of letters from U.S. parent corporations.

Economic Council of Canada This I submit, Mr. Chairman, is the measure of the problem that this government and this economic planning commissioner are going to have to face. The way Canada's economy is flowing now, it is nothing short of a running hemorrhage. The dominion bureau of statistics tells us that in 1958 the net outflow from Canada was $444 million; in 1959 it had risen to $491 million; in 1961 it had risen to $561 million, and in 1962 to $570 million. Nor is this the whole story, Mr. Chairman, because in addition to these enormous sums that are draining from the Canadian economy to the United States, there are vast reinforcements of surplus earnings in this country by these foreign corporations to expand their already enormous assets in this country.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that no planning commission, no government, is going to be able to deal with our economic problems unless it is prepared to face up to this major circumstance regarding Canada. It is not too much to say, sir, that the Canadian economy has now become a joke and a fraud; that it is a hollow shell. We have built around it, or rather have allowed to develop within that shell, industries, resource exploitation entirely in foreign hands. We surround this shell with national institutions such as this parliament, provincial legislatures, even our police forces, and all the other amenities of national life. Actually, they are enclosing an almost completely foreign body at this date.
I suggest to you that this is the major point of attack that this government is going to have to make with its economic planning commission. It will not achieve that purpose by anything in the nature of indicative planning. It is not much use telling people that they ought, really, to relinquish these things to the nationals of the country in which they operate; that would be the nice thing to do. What they are interested in is what would be the profitable thing to do. Any planning commission that is going to have the slightest effect on economic development in Canada is going to need to exercise coercive power, and this is one of the points at which its coercive powers will have to be exercised if Canada is not to become a political as well as an economic and military satellite of the neighbouring republic.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister) moved
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure (a) to establish a department of industry to be presided over by a minister of industry who shall be appointed under the great seal of Canada, to authorize the appointment of a deputy minister by the governor in council, and to provide for the appointment to the department on a temporary basis of persons having special knowledge of manufacturing industries to assist in the work of the department; (b) to provide for the establishment under the direction of the minister of an area development agency and to provide for the appointment of a commissioner and a deputy commissioner for area development; and (c) to make a consequential amendment to the Salaries Act to provide a salary for the minister.

Mr. Chairman, we have just passed a resolution which makes possible the introduction of a bill dealing with an economic council for Canada, and we have just given first reading to the bill that would establish that council. The test of the value of the economic council's work will be whether it succeeds in identifying what I might refer to as the emerging points of expansion in our economy and to help keep our economy expanding to a point where it will be able to' provide for full employment. Its task will also be to guide the public and the government, and give advice on what are the sectors of our economy from which we can expect strong: expansion, and what are the things that a growing Canada can produce in greater quantity and for the nation's benefit.
What can we do now that will help us to make the most of our resources and our talents, and how can we adopt our economy to changing conditions? Those are the problems and the work of an economic council and, as I said earlier this afternoon, the point of all this is to help government and all the various sectors of the economy to work together.
The point and purpose of the department of industry, which it is proposed to set up, will be to assist in transmitting these various ideas into effective action. We have a Department of Agriculture responsible for the action that government can take to help farmers. We have a Department of Fisheries which performs
802	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department the same function for fishermen. For the mining industry we have the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. However, Mr. Chairman, there is no department of industry, no department of government especially concerned with the needs and the opportunities of manufacturing industry, and the main purpose of the resolution before us now is to remedy that fact. The bill that we seek leave to introduce is one to create a department which will be for manufacturing industry what the Department of Agriculture is for farmers.
Specifically, the functions of the new department will be to maintain close, practical contact with industry, to make sure that industry gets service from government. It will be a department to which manufacturers can come to find out what is going on, to get advice and help in their problems. New and expanding enterprises in particular will look to it to see that government policies make their paths as smooth as possible. It will be concerned with translating into specifics the more general ideas about our economic growth that we hope will be generated in the economic council.
It will review, industry by industry, what can be done to increase Canadian production and how government can help in this regard. It will do this against the background provided by the longer term prospects assessed and analysed by the economic council, but in its own operations as a department it will be concerned with the building rather than the blueprints of an expanding economy.
In proposing to set up such a department we are not, of course, writing on a clean slate. We will not be introducing a whole new range of government activity. Much of the machinery that the new department will use is already in existence in one form or another. It exists particularly in various sections of the Department of Trade and Commerce and in the Department of Defence Production, which would be absorbed by the new department of industry if that department is set up.
In introducing this measure the government has no intention of setting up a great new bureaucratic machine, duplicating work already being done and some of which would be continued. Whenever possible existing organizations, existing services and existing people will be used. This does not mean, naturally, that nothing will be added. In some measure, indeed in relatively small measure, this must be and will be done. That is why the resolution provides for temporary appointment to the department of people who are not civil servants but who have special knowledge of manufacturing industries. It is hoped such appointments will bridge the


transition stage until the department can be fully staffed by the standard methods of recruitment. Full staffing, however, will not mean heavy staffing. The work for which this new department is designed is not work that should require a lot more people in Ottawa.
What is at present lacking in government organization is not activity connected with industry so much as a focus point that will give clarity and direction to government action to encourage industry, and in asking the house to consider this legislation we are asking it to provide such a focus.
I can hardly overemphasize the importance which we in the government attach to the creation of this new department. What-and this bears on the work of the new department very directly, and on its responsibilities- what are to be the sources of the new wealth and employment which Canada needs? Where are we going to provide the jobs for the 250,000 young people by which our labour force is going to increase in each of the next few years? That, I may add, does not take into consideration the amount of immigration which we would like to see coming to Canada.
Where will we find, in addition, the new jobs that are needed to keep pace with automation and other technological changes- changes which mean that our existing level of production will require fewer workers in existing industries? What will be the sources of increased exports we must make in order to pay for necessary imports and at the same time strengthen our payments balance with other countries which at present and for some years has been in dangerous imbalance?
There is no doubt about the answer, in general terms, to these questions. It is clear, however, that in trying to find specific answers we have to accept the fact that manufacturing industry, secondary industry, is the source from which the new wealth and the new employment must largely come. The development of Canada in the past has been built largely on our farms and our great raw material producing industries. They are not going to shrink, even though the number of men required to operate them may shrink, as it has over the years. But they themselves, in their production of wealth, are not going to shrink. Our soil, forests and mineral resources will continue, of course, to contribute very importantly to our development, but for the future expansion that we need if we are to take care of our work force we must now look especially to the manufacturing industries.
In the past government encouragement of manufacturing industry in Canada has been closely linked, in many people's minds-and

there is some evidence to support the linking -with policies of protectionism. The main way to help our industries often seemed to be to build a tariff wall around our relatively small domestic market. But whatever the historical justification for that attitude-and it is not difficult to find some historical justification for it-there is now, I think, widespread recognition that it does not fit the industrial needs of the 1960's. Our aim today cannot be simply to build up industry, any kind of industry in a general way, by general action. Canada's need is for industries that will thrive in the modern world, industries that will fit into the new patterns of international trade which are now emerging and to which we will have to adapt ourselves. There are signs that industry is adapting itself to these changes. We must strengthen our international payments balance, but we cannot expect to do so by cutting down imports of some of the simpler kinds of manufactured goods which more and more countries are now able to produce for themselves and sell economically. Our special need in this country-and this applies to other highly developed industrial countries-is to create and expand the more sophisticated, the more complicated, if you like, kinds of industry producing goods which we both need ourselves and which we can sell to other countries. Such export markets will need to include, increasingly, the developing countries, the new countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America, which should be the fastest growing markets for the most advanced kinds of industrial products that we in this country are increasingly able to produce efficiently and economically. We will not make this kind of progress, this increase, by industrial protectionism. So the aim of the department we propose will not be to shelter or shoreup weak, protected enterprises but to encourage and build up economic industries and to help industries adapt themselves and, in certain cases, adjust themselves to changes which are being made.
The debate on this resolution is, of course, not the occasion for me to go into more detail about the organization of the proposed department. That can only be done when the bill is before us. But there are two points which I think it is appropriate for me to mention in connection with this resolution before I sit down. We all recognize, I am sure, the deep and intimate concern with the welfare of industry that is felt by the governments of the provinces. That is their constitutional responsibility as well as their natural duty. The establishment of a federal department of industry will in no way lessen or interfere with provincial responsibilities. The new federal department will not in any way
7,	1SG3
Establishment of Industry Department create new federal responsibilities. Its concern will be simply and solely to discharge more efficiently and effectively the responsibilities which already fall on federal authorities. By providing a purpose for federal action, I believe the new department will make it easier for provincial departments of industry to do their work. Therefore, far from being hampered or interfered with, provincial action in support of industry will be, we hope, assisted by this development. Opportunities for fruitful federal-provincial co-operation will be improved.
In this respect, Mr. Chairman, I would mention particularly the area development agency which is proposed as an important part of the new department. The areas we are concerned with are those in which unemployment is heavy and chronic in its nature, where special government action is therefore called for in order to encourage economic development or industrial adjustment. Various departments of the federal government can be helpful in different ways to such areas. The purpose of the proposed area development agency is to assist in making sure that this will be done. It will create in Ottawa a small group of people whose special responsibility, on behalf of the minister of industry, will be to make sure that various federal policies are conceived and co-ordinated in ways which will be of maximum help to the areas of maximum need. Again, the point is to make action more effective by providing a focus for it. In this sense the area development agency will be co-ordinating rather than executive. In this way it will not interfere with provincial action to the same end. Quite the contrary. If the coordination and effectiveness of federal action are improved, action by the provinces in their areas of responsibility will become easier to take and will be made more fruitful.
In proposing this measure, Mr. Chairman, the government is by no means blind to the difficulties and problems which will arise and which the new department, if it is set up, will have to face. But the need, it seems to us, for a department of this kind has mounted rapidly with the changing nature of the Canadian economy and the growing relative importance of manufacturing industry in that economy as a provider, especially of jobs. The time has come when some of the difficulties in the way of expansion and employment must be surmounted. I believe that a department of this kind can help in that regard. There are now before our economy both challenges and opportunities which, I suggest, the creation of a department of industry can assist in solving and exploiting.

Establishment of Industry Department I think this will be a forward step and one which it is important to take now. I hope the house will agree to deal in that spirit with the resolution which I now have the honour to propose.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee has listened with interest and its usual attention to the words of the Prime Minister in bringing forward this resolution to create a new department of government. There are various attitudes one could take in connection with this, but time does not permit me this afternoon to deal thoroughly with the various aspects which I am sure impress each and every one of us, the possibilities, perhaps advantages and problems in connection with this resolution. At least we have seen today an example of co-operation among the various opposition parties and the government in moving ahead very rapidly with one resolution this afternoon. Perhaps I can therefore be pardoned for not coming too quickly to definitive statements with respect to this resolution in the next 18 minutes which still lie ahead of me on the clock. We have in the resolution we have already dealt with-the one setting up the economic council-I am not going to interpret the actions which may have prompted the government and the Prime Minister in bringing forward that resolution, but as I read in the speech from the throne, the control of that council is going to lie in the hands of another minister, the president of the privy council. I think there is a real problem in the relationship of the departments of government. I think

I am speaking now not of immediate past history, and certainly not of contemporary events, but I think anyone who has read the political history of this country and, where the same factors apply, in others, will find, not conflicts, but pressures arising between different departments as to which one is going to have control of the economy, particularly over fiscal and financial matters necessary for the solution of those problems.
It may be fair to say that on this question too-and, again, I am not speaking, as I said, of the contemporary scene or of the immediate past, of which I have had some experience -there may have been conflicts-pressures, rather, not conflicts-between, let us say, the Department of Finance and the Department of Trade and Commerce. When you have departments headed by strong ministers-and they have been headed by strong ministers in the past, we all know that these ministers, together with their departmental officials do, quite properly, suggest that the solution of the nation's problems lies in their department handling the affairs immediately before the nation. Whether that is the reason why, in


connection with the economic council, the Prime Minister took it upon himself to move the resolution rather than allow one of the other ministers to do it is a matter, of course, the secrets of which I am not conversant with in any way. I do not know.
I, perhaps have had a little experience in a minor way of similar pressures. I know this presents a real problem. But at least here we have had a solution arrived at, apparently, which, if I read the speech from the throne correctly, gives us the worst of all worlds. We are to have this council controlled by another minister, the President of the Privy Council, rather than by, say the Minister of Finance who, one might well think is best suited, for a number of reasons, for this position. After all, the Minister of Finance, must take a certain responsibility for financial and fiscal matters; otherwise, he cannot carry out the duties which rest on him. But in this case the proposed department will come neither under his jurisdiction nor under that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is the President of the Privy Council who is to administer this branch of the government. We have been told this afternoon-and I believe we are all thankful to know this- that it is only to be an advisory council, not one with any managerial capacity or power of direction. Perhaps the same problem arises again in connection with this department the resolution concerning whose establishment the Prime Minister introduced to-this committee a few minutes ago.
It could be argued in various ways. I have had some little experience with this. I remember that in days gone by pressure was brought to bear, not pressure, but suggestions in briefs, by various delegations, not least among them by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, which wanted a separate department of trade and industry. As I recall it latterly, or in the last two or three years during which I have had some experience in the matter, the suggestion was not that we should have a separate department of trade or industry but that we should change the name to that of trade and industry. With that suggestion, I am sure, we were all in full accord. With all due respect to the department, which has accomplished a great deal and which has been well managed and well run throughout the years, perhaps the name "trade and commerce" was something of a misnomer. It led those associated with manufacturing to feel they were being ignored. The suggestion was, apparently, of selling and buying rather than of manufacture. That did suggest that the name of the department should be changed and that it should be called the department of trade and industry. I think that is a proposition.

the logic of which would appeal to everyone. To move from that, from a change of name, to the creation of two departments, a department of trade and a department of industry, is something to which this committee should, I think, pay very careful attention and be satisfied only after very strong arguments before it accepts the principle which, no doubt, will be put forward in detail in the bill.
I can see trade and I can see industry. I think they go hand in hand. If you manufacture apple sauce you are in industry. If you manufacture a can you are in industry. If you put that apple sauce into the can you are on the verge of industry and trade. And when you start to sell it you are in trade or industry, I presume, and the sauce may go sour in the meantime. I think there is a real problem here to decide where industry stops and where trade begins. I think we have had very strong and able men running the Department of Trade and Commerce going back at least over my experience in this House of Commons, which I entered on the same day as the right hon. Prime Minister. We are among the seniors in this house at the moment.
Just young fellows.

Thank you very much. We had the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe as minister of trade and commerce, and the department has, I think, been well run and well managed. It has contributed a great deal to the welfare of the Canadian economy, at least during the years I have been here and undoubtedly many years before that. I wonder just what benefit would accrue to the Canadian economy, to Canadian efficiency and to departmental efficiency if we were now to have a bifocal department with a minister of trade on one side and a minister of industry on the other. I am not expressing any views at the moment. I am simply raising problems which I think are being raised by this measure. Certainly, to some extent we are emasculating the Department of Trade and Commerce; we are splitting it up. I am willing to hear arguments and I am sure we shall hear them when the government, later, sees fit to bring this bill forward for a second reading. I am sure we shall hear arguments as to why this should be done. I can assure the Prime Minister and the committee that as far as I am concerned I would want to hear very logical and cogent arguments advanced before I would welcome-though we may have to accept-the provision which is apparently envisaged in the resolution which is before us this afternoon.
As to the overlapping of the departments, the Prime Minister, speaking on this a few
7. 1983
Establishment of Industry Department minutes ago, referred and, possibly, he was ranging over the whole field as I, perhaps, am doing at the moment, to the problem of protection. He said this department should not foster protection in every way possible in a free economy, and so on, as we all do. Well, of course, the subject of protection and tariffs has been debated in this house ever since the original peace tower was built .-perhaps not so far back as that, because it was built in 1865; but ever since the first parliament met here in 1867-and, undoubtedly, it has been discussed ever since. As one wag said, there was a great disagreement between the parties. The Liberal party did not want tariffs to go any higher, and the Conservative party did not want them to go any lower, and on that they had a common ground on which they could agree. Anyway, this has been the cause of bitter argument and criticism in debate in days gone by. But as to the subject of protection, I think, with all due respect that you get advice from your colleagues in the cabinet as a whole. But in the end-perhaps I have an affinity with that department-I think the Minister of Finance has to be largely responsible for recommending to his colleagues fiscal and financial policy, and with all due respect to whoever may be the minister of this newborn fledgling which is to be brought forth, the parentage of which is a little uncertain at the moment, I should hate to think he would be responsible for dealing with fiscal and financial matters.
Mr. Chairman, one could go into many things in discussing this question, but as I said, at the moment I am simply pointing out the difficulties which lie before the committee, the government and the house before we are all in agreement on the acceptance of this principle. We have a very highly trained staff in the Department of Trade and Commerce. The government with which I had the honour of working created a small business section with special assistance given to the development of trade and industry. I would suggest with all due respect to the Prime Minister-and I would be surprised if the civil servants who were associated with the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) did not agree-that there was tremendous progress made in the development of industry in this country in the last two, three or four years, not only the last year to which reference has been made. The Prime Minister admitted development in the gross national product, but the foundation for that, at any rate, was laid before the last year. There had been a constant but perhaps not as sensational a development as there was last year, and that came, not under

Establishment of Industry Department the aegis of the government as a whole but the Department of Trade and Commerce, perhaps misnamed as it was.
Personally, Mr. Chairman, I cannot accept the argument that in order to get a development of industry in this country we now have to have a bifocal approach, that we have to split the two departments. The Prime Minister was careful to say that we are not going to have many officials. We are going to borrow, we are going to ask for assistance, and we are not going to create a further bureaucracy in this country. But with all due respect, in spite of the administrative genius of the minister who it is suggested will head this department as, if and when this parliament creates it, and the administrative abilities of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, I suggest that Parkinson's law is inexorable and inevitable, and whether you borrow them, beg them or steal them you will have an increase of bureaucracy every time in any event. You have it every day, Mr. Chairman, and you are going to have it to a greater extent than ever before with the creation of other departments.
There are other matters of legislation on the order paper in this connection which are not germane to this debate at the moment-[DOT] further creation of departments or bifocal departments. The whole tendency is in the further creation and extension of a bureaucracy which I do not think is at all in keeping with the stated desire of the government to improve its efficiency, to reduce its costs, and all the rest of it. As I said, there has been a tremendous development taking place in the last few years.
The Prime Minister referred a few moments ago to the balance of payments and his hope that we could reduce the deficit still further. He stated, quite properly, that we could not do it by narrow, insular protectionism but by an increase in our exports and an increase in our economy generally. There again, Mr. Chairman, the record shows that during the last year, in reducing the deficit in the balance of payments we made a greater advance than has occurred since some time in the early 1950's. That was done by the concerted effort of all branches of the government, and it was done to a substantial extent under the aegis and the leadership of the then ministers of trade and commerce, in association with their colleagues in the cabinet. So, as I say, I cannot accept this principle. I need further evidence than I have had today if we are to accept this government policy.
We are not going to filibuster a matter such as this. We are going to study these measures
[Mr. Nowlan.l

as they come forward. We are going to criticize them, try to improve them and amend them as our experience and advice would suggest. The responsibility ultimately rests on the government, but I for my part cannot see the necessity for one moment for splitting the department of trade and the department of industry. There were verbal, token arguments suggested by the Prime Minister a few moments ago, but I think he has to go much further than that before he and his colleagues can convince this committee, this house and the country that this further excursion into bureaucracy is not an expense and a duplication of effort, and is I suggest inefficiency rather than efficiency.
Mr. Chairman, I have not time at this moment to refer to the other department or branch mentioned in this resolution which is before us to provide under the direction of the minister for an area development agency. That is a very worthy purpose, Mr. Chairman. We have heard of area developments throughout the years. I suggest that the record of the immediately preceding government in dealing with these matters and in dealing with, shall we say, tax incentives to encourage the location of industry-and various other measures have also been implemented by the provincial governments-is commendable. I read in the paper today of another example where in the province of Nova Scotia, which of course is one of the provinces which has given the lead to Canadian development, since January of this year there have been eight or nine new industries brought into the province by the agency of the provincial government, the Industrial Estates Limited. I think, Mr. Chairman, that an agency such as that can be more effective in dealing with area development in certain areas than undertaking it on a national basis.
However, as I said, this resolution is one which I think has great importance and is worthy of the most careful consideration and study by this committee and the house. I should now like to call it five o'clock.

subtopic: PROVISION RESPECTING CONTROL OP CONSUMER CREDIT
PROVISION RESPECTING CONTROL OP CONSUMER CREDIT
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-6, to provide for the control of consumer credit.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in introducing this bill for consideration on second reading I should like to deal with it in four phases: first, the purpose of the bill; second, the need for regulation of this kind in the field of consumer credit; third, the degree of interest in this whole subject that has been displayed by members in all parts of the house and, fourth, what appears to be a very genuine need for an examination of the whole field of finance companies and consumer credit and other forms of lending in Canada as a whole. The explanatory note sets out the main purposes of the bill. First, it is intended that persons, institutions and companies engaged in the lending of money shall be compelled to disclose to the borrower the actual amount of interest being charged and at the time of making of the loan a statement shall be furnished to the prospective borrower setting out in detail the total amount of the unpaid balance on which interest is being charged, the total amount of interest payable under the agreement, whatever the agreement may be, and the actual relationship between the principal and the total amount of interest that is being paid.
All of -us who have had any dealings with contracts and agreements involving the payment of interest are well aware of the fact that there are, of course, many reputable companies engaged in this field of activity who quite accurately set forth the amount of interest they are charging their customers, but there are also a large number of companies who manage to conceal very carefully in their agreements the actual amount of interest to be paid with the consequent result that many of the borrowers have no idea whatsoever as to the true amount of interest which they are being charged. Under these agreements interest can vary anywhere from 6 to 26 per cent.
The bill seeks further to broaden the definition of an agreement to include deeds, assignments, mortgages, agreements for sale, conditional sales agreements, chattel mortgages and any instrument or contract involving the levying of interest on money being lent. Section 4 of the bill seeks to impose an upper limit of 10 per cent interest which may be charged. Section 5 of the bill states that in any case where the lender fails to give an accurate statement to the borrower the agreement shall be void with respect to the payment of interest. Section 28902-5-52i
Control of Consumer Credit 6 states that whenever the rate of interest charged exceeds 10 per cent the contract will be void in that regard.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, the main purpose of the bill is an attempt to let borrowers of money know precisely and accurately what they are being charged and to impose upon lenders of money the duty of making the interest rate perfectly clear and simple to the borrower at the time the loan is made. The need for some detailed regulation in this line of activity is only too evident. A recent issue of the Globe and Mail on March 3 of this year discusses a speech made by Dr. Jacob Ziegel, professor of law at the University of Saskatchewan. In his remarks Dr. Ziegel outlined to his audience that at the end of 1962 there was $4 billion outstanding in Canada on consumer credit loans of one kind or another. He went on to say that this amounts to approximately $210 for every man, woman and child in Canada at the present time.
So, Mr. Speaker, the field of consumer credit is an enormous one and embraces activities from coast to coast in Canada. For example, the dominion bureau of statistics estimates that as of March 31 there was $3,664 million outstanding in various forms of consumer credit. This is broken down into various categories. For example, conditional sales agreements total $771 million, small loans $658 million, home improvement loans $67 million and personal bank loans $1,206 million. It goes through all the statistics and points out very conclusively the tremendous market that exists in Canada in the field of consumer lending, the consequent need that follows for a very careful examination of the rules and regulations governing this field, and in particular the degree to which borrowers of money are protected and made aware of the circumstances and the rates at which they are doing the borrowing.
To refer back to Dr. Ziegel, he registers the complaint that credit can be obtained too easily and says that advertisers should be made to give all the details of credit buying plans in their advertisements. I do not think there is any doubt that there is a great deal of activity in Canada in this particular field of lending and it is one in which the rules and regulations governing it are somewhat nebulous and dispersed.
With respect to the degree of interest in this whole field, if we examine the order paper before us today it is evident that this particular field of activity has been given considerable attention by members on all sides of the house. We have on the order paper order No. 4 in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) amending the Small Loans Act, order No. 5 in the name

Control of Consumer Credit of the same member to amend the Interest Act, order No. 9 in the name of the same member to amend the Small Loans Act, order No. 18 in the name of the hon. member for Roverval (Mr. Gauthier) to amend the Small Loans Act, order No. 26 in the name of the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Nasserden) to amend the Interest Act, order No. 50 in the name of the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) to amend the Interest Act and order No. 57 in the name of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) respecting relief against unconscionable transactions.
It is obvious, therefore, that this is a field in which members of the house in all parties have taken a great deal of interest and no doubt many more bills would have been placed on the order paper by other members had it not been that these bills probably cover the areas in which they are interested. I merely point that out in passing to say that what I should like to initiate today is not so much a discussion on the specific proposals of this bill, which I must admit is somewhat limited, but rather to initiate a general discussion in the house in the coming weeks on the whole broad field of consumer credit and the institutions and organizations that handle this type of financing in Canada.
It may well be that it is not sufficient merely to designate that lending companies must make clear to prospective borrowers the actual interest rate they are being charged, nor will it be sufficient to pass legislation protecting purchasers from unconscionable transactions. Both these aims are very laudatory and necessary but it seems to me that one thing we have to do is to go one step further and decide if it is not about time that we had in Canada legislation governing these small loans companies and making certain that they make full disclosure to the public not just of the amount of interest they are charging but actual information as to the principles behind these companies and the degree of soundness of these organizations. It may well be that laws and regulations will have to be passed to set up controls over these lending institutions.
Various organizations in Canada are already requesting such action. In the Financial Post of February 16 last an article appears entitled "10%ers Under Squeeze". This article is devoted to the problem created in Canada by the new lending institutions that have been set up which are not subject either to provincial or federal regulation because they lend money on notes running for less than 365 days. The trust companies and the various banking institutions have called for effective legislation at the federal and provincial levels that will provide protection for the public where none now exists. The article goes on,


of course, to outline the constitutional problems involved in that under the British North America Act the federal government has power over interests and banking but the provinces have legislative power over matters of property and points out that there seems to be an area here where some co-operation is going to be required.
The particular article in question states that the public have no need at the present time of distinguishing between the type of institution which is subject to government inspection and audit, and those that are not so regulated. This particular article actually suggest the creation of a federal financial institution's act covering all of these types of lending institutions and regulating their profits and their method of operation in the Canadian economy.
An article in the Financial Post of March 16 discusses a particular firm of this character and recites how it makes no disclosures at all as to its financial worth, as to earnings or the make-up of its organization. Yet, this firm advertises widely throughout the province of Ontario, borrowing money and guaranteeing to pay it back. The borrower has no idea as to the nature of the institution or whether it, in fact, has assets of substance with which to carry out its obligations.
There are many such articles, as I have said. It is interesting to note, for example, that in the United Kingdom, the House of Commons has actually passed and is awaiting third reading, a bill called the protection of depositors bill. This bill is designed to give protection to those people who place deposits with these types of financial institutions I have just mentioned. An article in the Financial Post of March 2, outlines in great detail the limitations that are placed on these various institutions.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, there are many articles of this kind suggesting that institutions in Canada that are engaged in the small loans business-many of them of course are quite reputable-are fleecing the public. They do not make disclosures of the actual amounts of interest they are charging, nor do they tell the public the nature of their own assets and liabilities so that one can judge whether they are sound enough to risk one's money.
I do not want to speak at length on this subject, Mr. Speaker, except to suggest, after looking through the order paper, there seems to be very considerable interest shown by all members in the house in this particular field of consumer credit and small loans, the financing of appliances and other matters of that sort. It seems to me that rather than have these bills come up continually during the session to be debated for one hour, it

might be possible to devise some method of referring all the bills, holus-bolus, to the standing committee. If this could be done, all these matters could be considered at one time. Witnesses could be heard, the presidents of these various loan companies could have the pleasure of appearing before us, speaking themselves and being cross-examined, the various local officers of the crown could give us their opinions as to the necessity for legislation covering these institutions. Perhaps the law officers could guide us concerning the appropriate type of legislation to introduce. I have mentioned to some of my friends across the way that in the one hour we have for private bills we obviously cannot debate in any great detail the necessity or desirability of entering into this whole field.
However, it does seem to me that there is a great need for action in this regard. There is a vacuum in our legislation at the present time. There is a widespread opinion among private members in the house that this field should be investigated. I think instead of talking each bill out as it comes up, some method could be found by which to refer this whole matter of consumer credit and financing to a committee of the house, where all members could discuss it. Perhaps a composite bill could be drafted which would embrace the ideas of all private members' bills now before the house. Then, at some later time we could bring back to the house a composite bill which would protect consumers in the purchases they make, a bill that would allow the people of Canada to know where they stand with these companies, a bill that would force these companies to lay all their cards before the committee. I feel that if we could do this at this or some future session, we would be rendering a service to the people of Canada as a whole.
