In rising to join in this debate, I wish to commend the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) for introducing this bill. It is timely. As he has indicated, interest in this subject is fashionable. When one looks at the order paper, he finds an extraordinary percentage of private members' bills concerning this general subject. I have noticed the following bills: Bills Nos. C-6; C-9; C-10; C-12; C-14; C-23; C-31; C-33; C-43; C-45; C-55, and C-62. These private members' bills come from all corners of the house and the sponsors of them represent the four political parties here, as well as all parts of Canada.
Most of these bills have much in common. I do not believe this is an easy subject with which to deal. The hon. member for Danforth has referred to a very difficult subject, a
Control of Consumer Credit subject we have to consider in conjunction with a good deal of other legislation within federal jurisdiction. For example, when I was looking through the index I noticed the Interest Act, chapter 156; the Small Loans Act, chapter 251; the Loan Companies Act, chapter 170; the Bank Act, chapter 12 of the revised statutes of 1952. Then, there is the Co-operative Credit Association Act, 1952-53, chapter 28, and the Bills of Exchange Act, chapter 15 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. All these measures have a bearing on this subject. I am reminded of the contribution that was made to the debate last night by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) when he spoke on another private bill. The hon. member, speaking not only from experience on the treasury benches but from experience in business and law, indicated the broad ramifications that there are to some of these bills directed to other legislation.
Of course, these private bills would not be here if the Canadian public was not concerned about consumer credit and its ramifications. I think the subject is even more timely from the standpoint of the province of Ontario because of a case of historic interest in connection with the unconscionable transactions relief act. The case is that of Re Sampson and Barfried Enterprises Ltd. The decision is a decision of the court of appeal and the court was composed of Chief Justice Porter, and Justices MacKay, Schroeder, Kelly and McLennan. The hearing was on October 15, 1962, and I think the decision may have a bearing on this whole subject. I should like just to read the headnote:
"Interest" as a class of subject within exclusive federal competence under Section 91(19) of the B.N.A. Act is a precise and unambiguous term, and in the absence of any contrary indication should be expounded in its natural and ordinary sense. It is not restricted to compensation determinable by application of a rate per centum to the principal amount of a loan, but covers compensation for the use of money by way of a fixed sum whether denominated a bonus, discount or premium, provided it is referable to principal money or to an obligation to pay money.
Any member who is interested in this particular aspect of the law should refer to it. What it does indicate is that the Ontario act upon which we have relied for some years, the unconscionable transactions relief act, revised statutes of Ontario, 1960, chapter 410, is ultra vires.
That means therefore we are compelled to address ourselves to the problem, not only because of current business and financial conditions in the country, but certainly in Ontario because the remedies upon which we have been accustomed to rely are no longer there. I think some of us are somewhat surprised as to the breadth of that decision, because in

Control of Consumer Credit law school we were of the view that too large federal dependence on the interest power might not be constitutional. We tended to think that property and service rights were the exclusive property of the province. This case is not in dispute because apparently this decision did not go to the Supreme Court of Canada. Unfortunately we are without a supreme decision on this matter, but we must take into account the likelihood that the federal parliament is responsible in this area more than we had thought.
As the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) has indicated, consumer credit legislation is of interest not only to Canada but throughout the world. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I was interested to read the history of this kind of legislation in the United States, where there has been developed a large body of experience in small loans and sales on a credit basis. It would appear there are essentially two basic philosophies with respect to control of credit sales.
One philosophy is that the most important thing is to compel full disclosure of essential facts concerning an instalment credit transaction, it being felt that the consumer, being able to recognize the difference in cost and services and relying on the competitive processes of supply and demand, will be able to act wisely; but there is another view which seems to come into a great deal of proposed legislation in different places, the view that statutory limitations on financial charges should be imposed, and in this bill the hon. member has proposed both. I personally would feel that the second is somewhat less commendable than the first.
I know that the hon. member who proposed this bill is a graduate in honour economics, and I think he would agree with me that legislation cannot increase a volume of money supply to be borrowed, and we can only accomplish so much by setting statutory limits. What really do we accomplish by setting an arbitrary limit of 10 per cent beyond which rates will not be pushed? Certainly it does not create any more money available for credit. Perhaps the philosophy behind this is that there should not be anything lent above that figure. I do not care to express any particular view on this matter, but when I looked at the private members' bills filed, I noticed that in many of the bills proposed here there is concentration on the disclosure aspect, but not generally the same emphasis as in this bill on the establishment of a rate.
Only recently an important bill was introduced in the other place by Senator David Croll, which attracted considerable public attention. That bill, which of course is familiar to my hon. friend from Danforth, Bill S-6, is an act to make provision for the disclosure

of information with respect to finance charges. It was read the first time on Wednesday, May 22, 1963, and it pretty much follows models suggested in a number of foreign jurisdictions.
In the United States congressional committees have been concerned about this problem. Actually there, this is congressional concern which goes back to N.R.A. days under Roosevelt, and only recently President Kennedy has placed a great deal of emphasis on it again. As we know, the champion of this legislation in the United States has been Senator Paul Douglas and he has done a great deal to acquaint not only Americans but Canadians as well with the problem of credit legislation.
We find that with the introduction of this kind of legislation there are, of course, lobbies against it. This is something we would expect. One of the objections raised is that the mechanics of setting out rates is not nearly as easy as would appear in the simple language of the bill presently before us, which asks that the interest charge would be indicated. I have looked up an article in the Canadian Chartered Accountant of July 1962 which compares the accounting techniques for finance charges by several sales or finance companies. This is an article by an expert in the field, L. O. Morley, a chartered accountant, and he indicates some of the mathematics involved in various computations.
I think this is a pretty important question that should be considered by the appropriate committee of the house, and perhaps the suggestion made by the hon. member might be studied in the light of the experience of the American congressional committees. Certainly when we determine the methods by which financial charges are estimated we find there are a great many techniques-the cash method, the straight line method, the sum of the digits method, the average interest method and the use of arbitrary percentage. In fact as this article points out:
Such companies use none of the recognized methods but calculate the unearned balance of the finance charges by applying an arbitrary percentage to the total of instalment notes receivable at the balance sheet date.
Anybody who has been practising law knows how terribly difficult it is for an ordinary person to calculate what kind of charges there are, and of course this greatly adds to the complexity of good legislation on the subject.
I would just like to indicate that a bill which will be considered in due course, Bill C-31, introduced by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) is exactly the same as the bill before us, except that it adds a criminal penalty, whereas the bill introduced by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott)

provides a civil penalty in the sense that there will result a loss of the finance charges to the lender who fails to comply with the conditions set out in the bill.
Bill C-62, introduced by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) purports to fill a gap which is created by the Ontario decision to which I have referred which declared ultra vires the unconscionable transactions relief act of Ontario; so in a sense that hon. member is trying to do almost the same thing. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), who is an experienced member of the house proposes in Bill C-33 to amend the Bills of Exchange Act by limiting the negotiability of a bill of exchange given on an instalment purchase contract, and the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) in Bill C-55 would appear to be limiting the interest, defined broadly, to 12 per cent. The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) in Bill C-23 is trying to reduce the rate of interest or cost of a small loan from 2 per cent to 1 per cent per month.
Therefore I think the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) is quite correct when he indicates there is a wide interest in this and a resulting variety of attempts to do what would appear to be the same thing namely protect the consumer, particularly the unsophisticated consumer who cannot really know what he is paying. As we examine Bill C-10 we find this is a case of really doing something of the same, in this case limiting the interest charges to 12 per cent; and a number of other bills, Bill C-12 for example, which relates to bankruptcy, intends to incorporate some of the provisions of the Ontario unconscionable transactions relief act which, as I have indicated, has been ruled recently to be ultra vires.
So, we have this strange hodgepodge, of similar legislation coming within the purview of the federal parliament-the Small Loans Act, the Interest Act, the Loan Companies Act, the Bank Act, the Co-operative Credit Associations Act and the Bills of Exchange Act and I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it possible for any hon. member in this maze -and particularly in this confusion created by the recent Ontario case which purports to enlarge the real authority of the federal parliament-is it possible for any private member to solve this whole messy problem by one bill?
The bill proposed by Senator Croll attracted a great deal of interest, as I am sure that the bill which is now being discussed will attract further interest. Surely it is only on the basis of the gathering together of a great many reactions with regard to what is being done in this house, in the other place, in the United States or
Control of Consumer Credit Great Britain, where they have gone through very much this same problem since the end of world war II, that we can obtain the kind of information which is necessary in order to provide some sensible solution to the whole problem.
I feel, frankly, Mr. Speaker, that there ought to be an attempted consolidation in respect of a number of these interrelated acts. I do not understand how a lawyer today can give good advice when there are so many bills in the federal library and the provincial libraries which he has to consider. How can he possibly look up all the acts that relate to these important subjects?
The reactions to the Croll bill, which are fairly recent, show that there was almost universal support for the general principles of the bill. The house may recall that the Croll bill did not limit the percentage rate-I think he was perhaps wise in that-but it compelled disclosure. A number of economic studies that have been conducted in the United States seem to indicate that one of the advantages of compelling a clearcut statement of rate of interest charged is that it permits better competition to prevail. It does not limit moneys; it seems to increase moneys. One of the factors that tends to break down competition, I am told by some of these studies, is evidenced when the consumer was not in a position to shop around and make comparisons. I think that is perhaps the most valuable part of the hon. member's bill, the fact that there would be disclosure of the interest rate. How it should be done, I am sure I am not clever enough to suggest. As I have said, I have read these articles by chartered accountants who have made lifetime studies of this subject, and I know it is a very sophisticated subject and one which is going to call for the best ability that we have in our public service and among the hon. members of this house.
I agree with my hon. friend that this is the kind of legislation that could usefully be brought before our banking and commerce committee. I do not think this is a case of a witch hunt. I am quite sure there are many finance companies that are simply in business in a competitive way and are doing the best they can to give good service. At the same time I am satisfied that there are many sales of appliances where people do not know what is happening and are shocked when they ultimately learn what they have paid for a product. The Croll bill brought reactions from some people who had paid considerably more in interest than they had for the original appliances. This situation has became more serious over many years. Surely we must recognize that this situation prevails. Our hon. friends in the Social Credit party talk

Control of Consumer Credit about the dead hand of debt and the heavy-anchor of debt upon people in our economy. We agree on this important fact, that debt can be a terrible drag; it can be a drag which makes consumers in Canada feel unable to go out and purchase those things which they need now because they are still paying for something which they used up several years before.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we recognize that we cannot just cure this condition by passing a bill, but I think the hon. member is right in saying that a good bill at this time is one which will ensure more orderly consumer financing. But it has to be tied in, as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) suggested last night, with other legislation and business practice generally. This is important. Looking generally over the whole list of private members' bills, it seems to me that in broad terms there are two great focuses of interest and attention. The most important is-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the provisions of the bill now before us describe, as has already been said, a situation that has been concerning a great many hon. members of this house and of the other place for a number of years. I do not completely agree with all the provisions of this bill. However, I think it is well that it was introduced at this time so we may have a discussion respecting the whole matter of consumer credit, and so on. The hon. member mentioned that there has been a tremendous expansion in the amount of consumer credit during the past four years. I think the mover of the bill suggested that a recent survey showed there was something like $4 billion outstanding in consumer credit.
I think all hon. members will agree that if one looks around the country today he sees that there has been a tremendous proliferation, if I may call it that, of finance companies. Of course, when any phase or aspect of business expands rapidly it is usually because it is lucrative. I do suggest, however, that unless we re-examine some of the reasons which have led us into this situation, even the passing of this bill and perhaps several others which would offer some form of protection to the consumer would not solve the problem. It may, in fact, create more problems than it solves.
The Right Hon. Mackenzie King, one time leader of the party that is in power today, once said that usury, once in control, will

wreck any nation. I am wondering, because of the tremendous expansion of consumer credit and the concern expressed by so many hon. members by reason of there being so many bills of this type before us this session, whether we are not rapidly coming to the situation when we should take these words of wisdom into account and try to do something about it. There are dozens of cases known to each hon. member of this house where consumer credit and instalment buying of one kind and another have reached a point of diminishing return, a point of diminishing advantage, and in many cases individuals are in real difficulty because of the expansion of consumer credit.
Therefore I think the importance of having this debate this afternoon is that we can go back and make a brief examination of the factors leading up to the situation which we find today. I would suggest that we go back perhaps as far as 1939 or 1940 when the war started. This period was right at the end of what was then called a depression. They refer to these things as recessions now, but at least from that date up until the present time we have seen perhaps both ends of the spectrum of recession, depression, buoyancy, and so on. I think it is fair and safe to say that during the war there was a shortage of consumer goods and in fact there was a greater amount of purchasing power being distributed, through wages and profits, to the people of Canada than there were consumer goods available for purchase. Because of this there was a build up of savings-compulsory savings in some cases, but neverthless, savings, and more purchasing power going out than there were goods to be purchased. From 1946 to 1949 I suggest this consumer credit problem did not intrude itself and there was general prosperity throughout the country because those savings which had been accumulated during the war years were becoming active due to a greater supply of goods and services.
In 1949 there was another minor or major war effort, certainly not on the same scale as the 1939-1945 crisis, but again a large part of Canadian industry was put to work to produce war equipment. Wages and so on were being poured out and distributed into the economy for the production of something which never reached the consumer market. Here we had another expansion of purchasing power in respect of the production of goods which never did get on to the market. Along with this, from 1946 to 1955, there was also a tremendous expansion of industry all over Canada. Again, as long as this was going on, wages and earnings of one kind or another were being distributed to the people which, in turn, became purchasing power for something they were not bound to repay

immediately. It follows, of course, that the prices of goods would eventually contain a portion of the capital which had been necessary to bring about this industrial expansion in the first place. But as long as there was more money going out than was recovered in the prices of the goods being produced there was enough purchasing power, without the expansion of the consumer credit, to get the nation moving in reasonable prosperity, free from some of the problems we are now facing.
In 1955, or perhaps it was a few months before that, another phase began. Instalment buying and consumer credit began on a scale much greater than ever before. I think that by far the greatest proportion of those $4 billions which my hon. friend suggested just now as being outstanding as credit has arisen since 1955 or thereabouts. I believe it is also fair to suggest that this expansion in consumer credit is mortgaging our future income in order to pay for things which we as a nation have already produced. I think we can add to those $4 billion in consumer credit a large part of the expansion under C.M.H.C. and other agencies which do not show up as a consumer credit. This emphasizes the need to take a long, hard look at our financial and monetary system to see whether we cannot make some modification which would distribute fresh purchasing power through the Canadian people so that we, as a people, could collectively buy back those goods and services which we have produced without mortgaging our income for 20 years into the future. To implement the provisions of this bill, for example, to limit the amount of interest to 10 per cent, will not be effective unless we can find some way of seeing that purchasing power is distributed so that we can buy the things that industry produces.
I agree with those clauses of the bill which call for full disclosure of interest and other charges. I approve, also of some of the penalties provided for failing to make such disclosure. I feel, however, that if we were to accept this figure of 10 per cent per annum as the maximum rate of interest which could be charged-and even that is too high-the result might be the closing down of some of the consumer credit facilities which have been built up. This, in turn, could seriously affect purchases and slow down our industries still further. Thus, a very difficult problem has been raised by the sponsor of this bill, and 1 do not think the proposals made in this legislation are the solution. However, I do think that we as a parliament should seriously consider some modification in our monetary system to ensure that we do not arrive at our present situation again, and so
Control of Consumer Credit that we may rectify the situation in which we find ourselves at the present time.

I do not
intend, Mr. Speaker, to dwell at great length on this bill but I would like to say a few words about it.
First of all, I think there is no doubt that there is a great need for a serious study of this question. The fact that there are so many bills on the order paper on the subject, and the fact that so many people outside this house are concerned about consumer credit indicates clearly that there is need for something to be done in this field. In the second place, as the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) has indicated, the existing legislation in this field is overlapping.
As a layman trying to read through these books, I find the situation confusing. This is the second area of need-to straighten out and simplify the legislation which is already on the statute books. We have the Small Loans Act, the Interest Act, the Bank Act, a Loan Companies Act and an act involving unconscionable transactions. Where do these things fit together? It is difficult for the average person, the average consumer, to sort them all out. The fact is that there is great interest being shown on the subject on the one hand and confusion in the legislation on the other, which means that something must be done. I should like to confine my brief remarks to suggesting what might be done.
I do not want to look at the legislation. I want to think for a moment about what we are trying to achieve by this legislation, because we must do that, first of all, before we attempt to draft words. It is obvious that one basic problem exists, namely that the ordinary consumer in this country when he enters into a contract involving some form of interest payment does not know what he is buying. He has no idea what the interest rates are.. In some instances, consumers pay too much. They have no means of comparing one rate against another. Thus, I think it is clear that the first, the fundamental thing you must do, is arrive at legislation which will provide the consumer with facts, so that he may evaluate a contract and know what he is paying.
Having listened to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) I realize it is very difficult to state in concise terms just what the interest is. You can take a specific contract involving certain payments and get several accountants to look at it, and eventually come up with calculations which show the interest rate which applies to that contract.
This is a difficulty we will somehow have to resolve. Somehow we have to provide legislation so that first and foremost people

Control of Consumer Credit
know what they are buying and what the interest rates are. Then after that we have to look very carefully at whether or not we want to go beyond that step, whether or not we want to limit the interest chargeable. Again, I think we have reached the point that some people are unsophisticated in these matters, look at the interest, see what they are buying, and perhaps compare one contract against another which has the interest clearly stated. It still may not mean a great deal to them; and perhaps there is a point up to which we should provide protection by giving a statutory limitation to the interest to be charged. This is now done to some degree in the Small Loans Act with small loans.
Beyond that point, for business in general to try and restrict or limit the amount of interest which can be charged is wrong. I think there are people in business in this country who may need money for a special purpose for a relatively short term, perhaps under conditions of pretty high risk, and who are quite prepared to pay what to us is an abnormally high interest rate for the use of money. Should we legislate against their ability to do that? I do not think we should. I think if they know what they are doing and are prepared to do it, then in a free enterprise society we must allow an individual the right to make that sort of decision. When that point is reached we assume that the person entering into the contract knows what he is doing. At this point he has to fend for himself and make up his own mind, oased on the facts and his need as he sees it. Below this point we must provide some sort of protection. I think this is an area which requires a lot of thought, care and study before we rush through paper legislation which may be restrictive in areas in which it should not.
In winding up my remarks I should like to say that a need exists here. A study must be made. I hope this problem will be studied properly so that all the legislation is looked at. I hope it will be studied from the point of view of trying to put on paper some legislation which meets the kind of case I have tried to set out. I think those hon. members who have put this type of bill on the order paper have done us all a service by bringing this problem to the surface and letting it be discussed, and as a result of this I hope we will start to get some serious study started on the matter.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to mention one or two matters in connection with this bill. I agree with what the preceding speakers have said with regard to the need for some definite research
[Mr. Hahn.)
into this matter. What I should like to bring to the attention of the house is the relationship between the banking institutions we have today and the lending institutions. In this regard it has come to light that a line of credit established by lending institutions, such as finance companies, might be very large, and they may not be using that line of credit. An individual may go to a bank, ask for credit, and be turned down on the basis of a tight money policy. The very money that this individual should get from his banker is not available to him because of that tight money policy. Yet the lending institution or finance corporation may, through its very extensive line of credit, borrow the money from the bank and lend it to the individual. In this way, whereas the individual would have got his money at 6 per cent interest he is forced to pay finance company rates up to 24 per cent. Mr. Speaker, that is all I want to say because I do not want to talk the bill out.

The quotas for the twelve month period ending December 31, 1963, are as follows:
Waterproof footwear, 1,960,000 pairs; canvas footwear, 2,550,000 pairs.
